We can and must therefore specify the objects and concepts for which a language has words. We must identify what it has designated in words on earth and in the heavens, among lifeless and living things, in animal and human bodies, and finally among concepts of qualities and relations and among non-sensory concepts.

Where several languages have something in common, as the American languages do, even if only because the nations that speak them are similarly situated, it becomes important to see whether roughly the same domain encompasses the stock of concepts stamped into words in those languages. By comparing many languages, and always taking as our starting point that each offers a complete view of the world, we may well arrive at a domain of this kind that is, as it were, original and recurs in them all.

Indeed, since on the whole the same world presents itself to all nations, this domain would have to be the same for them all, were it not that the amount of this world actually transformed into language depends on capacity and opportunity.

Here it is easy to trace the progress of the discovery and naming of particular objects. It is especially important, however, to trace the modifications of concepts of the mind, a task that has still been pursued nowhere near precisely enough, even in familiar languages.

Within the vocabulary of a language a further question arises: which kinds of objects and concepts predominate in the richness of their expressions? Here too, then, it is important to distinguish them by class.

For differences naturally arise in this respect from the general level of cultivation of nations, and also from habits, customs and ways of life, which give a greater variety of expressions to one branch of human activity or another, and thus to one class of objects and concepts or another.

The general study of language must begin with the broadest classes and arrange its classification so as to show how language indicates the concept both to the understanding (§98) and to the ear. This may be called its technique of designation.

Since this requires us to follow language’s own course, and every need for designation has its basis in thinking, all words fall in this respect into those that concern the matter of thinking, its object, and those that concern its form, its activity.
For thinking needs words of its own to connect, separate and compare concepts, and to handle them according to its characteristic operations.

These words may be called logical or dialectical in general. Their distinctive feature is that, viewed subjectively, they designate what is produced by an inner act. Viewed objectively, they designate only the connections and relations of concepts and things to one another and to the understanding that thinks them, rather than objects or properties of objects.
The principal division in the matter of thought is naturally between the corporeal and the incorporeal.
For the technique of designation, however, another division, more fundamental in this respect, must come first, namely the division into words for objects, qualities and actions.

For objects always stimulate human beings through some salient feature of their quality or movement and thus prompt them to designate those objects chiefly by that feature. Hence words for qualities and movements stand highest in language as its most general words.
General words for relations and connections must also be counted here.

Strictly speaking, since it is the understanding that relates concepts to one another, these words fall into the class of expressions that designate its activity (§117). Yet insofar as the relations and connections are considered to be present in the objects themselves, the words belong here too.
One might object at this point that the distinction is merely grammatical.
In fact, it is both lexical and grammatical in all languages.

For in all languages there are words that are originally and by virtue of their concepts, hence lexically, nouns, adjectives and adverbs, or verbs, even without any grammatical markers. Grammar can then recast words belonging on this basis to one of the three classes into the other two.

It is essential to bear this in mind, for in more than one language non-original verbs are formed simply by combining an original verb with an equally original stem, hence by purely lexical means and without any help from grammar.
All the more particular divisions follow from these main divisions. I pass over them here, since I am trying to give as brief an outline as possible of the general structure of language.
The same classification of concepts also makes it easier to understand the technique of designation and furthers that understanding.

Here I shall stay within the domain of thinking (§98) and discuss this technique in terms of how words are chosen for things and concepts on the basis of other concepts singled out in them or brought into relation with them, leaving sounds aside.

These concepts are far from always discernible in the words. But it is exceedingly important to seek out those that can be discerned, since only then does the distinctive view of the world afforded by the language shine out clearly. Moreover, the whole way of designating through affinities among concepts, subjective and objective alike, is one of the most remarkable aspects of language.

For the task is nothing less than to rise from the earliest and crudest needs of mutual communication to the full range of the highest ideas and their finest shades, while always linking a new word or a new meaning to something already there. Language is always subject to the general condition that mutual understanding must be possible, so speakers may go beyond what is already understood only as far as their hearers can follow.

Language relates incorporeal concepts to corporeal ones, and the entities of the corporeal world to the general categories of quality and movement, though the second rule applies less consistently than the first.

It follows from both rules that language contains a number of general concepts of corporeal quality and movement that supply the principal material for designating all the others. These are therefore what one must particularly look for when investigating the vocabulary of a language.
This inquiry can accordingly proceed from two sides, that of the designating concepts and that of the concepts to be designated.

Comparing the results of these two procedures then shows the aptness of the designation and, in the selection and specification of the designating concepts, reveals the people’s prevailing inclination towards one mode of sensory viewing or another, as well as their mode of mental apprehension and its degree of clarity, precision, purity and depth.
It is therefore by no means necessary for a language to possess a number of root words that can be regarded as the source of all the rest.
Even where such words exist, derived words are also used, and used most frequently, to designate new concepts.
But the root words cannot be passed over here.
For they plainly have a twofold significance, grammatical and lexical.
In connected speech they can appear without grammatical alteration either not at all or only under certain conditions, and they serve as base words for derivation and compounding.
In some languages, such as Sanskrit and Welsh, it has become customary in lexicography to trace every word back to one of the posited roots.
Yet there is probably no language of this structure in which striking examples could not be found to show how unfounded such a procedure is.
Alongside the majority of words that lend themselves readily and easily to derivation from the roots, there are always many that can be brought under them only by forced and fanciful contrivance.
Language has another means of increasing the richness of its vocabulary besides forming individual expressions.
It marks features common to whole series of words and creates expressions by altering existing word sounds according to definite rules, without creating new word sounds.
This often takes place through simple compounding, but also through derivation, whether by agglutination or by inflection.

Examples include patronymics, names of clans or peoples, abstract nouns, words of possession (a class found in almost all American languages), causative and volitive verbs, and so forth. Since, for excellent practical reasons, it has become customary

to include in the grammar everything that can be reduced to rules and leave the dictionary only to list individual items alphabetically, these methods of designation are now usually found in grammars. They plainly belong, however, to the formation of the vocabulary rather than to the combining of words in speech.
A closer and deeper examination of them is important, for it allows us to judge how logically precise and philosophically sound the language’s procedure is.

For since we are dealing here with classes formed according to rules, what matters is how the basis of classification is conceived, whether all the kinds that follow from it are covered, and even whether chance or a rule governed the choice between designating these concepts by derivation, according to laws that must be learnt, and by compounding, in a way that is immediately intelligible.

For it would be more consonant with logical propriety to form words according to laws only where the kinds to be designated can be derived, in their number and character, from concepts alone, and to refrain from doing so where a particular factual relation determines the class of words, as with the concept of possession.

There is another case in which the logical aptness and completeness of linguistic designation must be tested. Where a set of concepts together fills an entire domain, the question is whether the language has a distinct expression for each and whether the expressions themselves mark the interrelation of the concepts.
Here I can give only the dimensions of space and the points of the compass as examples.

For the dimensions of space, several languages bring two distinct concepts under a single expression, as in *schmal* ‘narrow’ and *eng* ‘tight’, or *breit* ‘broad’ and *gross* ‘large’. For the points of the compass, the expressions in many languages, such as German and Sanskrit, preserve the uniformity of the concepts. German does so by reference to the course of the sun that divides the day, and Sanskrit by reference to an assumed standpoint from which the sides are determined. In other languages, such as Latin, this uniformity is disrupted or altogether absent.

The aim of this entire investigation of the vocabulary of languages, indicated here only in the barest outline, is to understand the system by which it is formed as precisely and completely as possible, so that one can see how much and what, out of the given range of possibilities, each language designates, and in what way.

One must therefore survey the domain of what is to be designated in its various divisions (§§113–118), the stock of concepts brought into relation with others for purposes of designation (§§119–122), and finally the range of word sounds in both root words and derived and compound words, with attention to the character and treatment of the sounds (§§73–82).

Once this is done, one has a conception of the material that language offers to speech, and all that remains is to consider the feeling that accompanies words (§105), their effect in turn on the mind.
So far this has been discussed only as part of the content of a word. Here we must consider together the distinctive way in which the language treats all its words.
Just as the world appears in what is to be designated, so the human being appears here, and the two are related to one another as they present themselves in one and the same language.

The greater or lesser readiness with which feeling is aroused, the lighter or darker colouring of the imagination, and the more prosaic or more poetic tendency emerge here as causes, just as they were recognized as effects in the objective formation of words.
It would therefore serve no purpose to go into greater detail here.

It is enough to observe that the vocabulary examined objectively up to this point must now be considered subjectively, to see whether a certain uniformity can be discerned in the feeling that prevailed in word formation and what kind of national distinctiveness is revealed in it.
For the feeling that acts on the formation of a word is the same feeling that always accompanies it afterwards in use.

I call it feeling partly to gather under the most general term everything in which language can bear traces of the human way of being, but chiefly because, at the moment it is active, what we are discussing really operates only as feeling, outside clear and distinct consciousness.

For in other respects it encompasses, most notably, the purely intellectual tendency, as well as the whole subjective effect that the words of a language produce by virtue of belonging to it and that differs from the effect produced by the words of another language.
It goes without saying that this effect in turn contributes to the language’s objective portrayal of the world.
Yet many distinctions and divisions that linguistic inquiry requires lead less to genuinely different objects than to the consideration of different aspects of the same object.

If, for example, the word formation of a language tends chiefly to keep the mind within the sphere of readily associating ideas for the purposes of life, it will above all be this intellectual disposition that ordinarily accompanies the language’s expressions for incorporeal things as well.
At the same time, this will lead those expressions themselves to apprehend their objects in designation from a more superficial aspect.
Nevertheless, to know the language fully in this respect, one must always consider together both this objective character and the subjective influence upon it.
For the latter will then appear in the same way in other parts of the structure of the language, notably in how words are joined in speech.

The subjective disposition that plays a part in forming a word and is in turn produced by the word once formed, since cause and effect continually change places, adheres far less firmly to the dead word than does the designation of the object.
If even the designation of the object is subject to change over time, as we have seen (§84), this holds far more strongly for the subjective impression.

Elevated words sink to the level of common ones, poetic words become prosaic, and vice versa. The whole direction of a nation’s thinking and feeling changes imperceptibly. As this in turn acts upon designation (§125), sound and meaning seem to stay the same and do so on the whole, yet the altered apprehension of the meaning discloses a difference in it to closer scrutiny.

In this way, expressions for incorporeal things in particular, such as *Seele* ‘soul’, *Geist* ‘spirit’, *Herz* ‘heart’ and *Gemüth* ‘mind in its affective aspect’, gradually acquire a very different sense simply through the way they are apprehended.

Conversely, when this happens in a few principal expressions, perhaps through the influence of individual writers, the nation’s cast of mind gradually changes, and this change then acts back on the entire language with increased force.
Individual words taken in isolation rarely bear any discernible traces of these changes in the feeling that accompanies them, whether or not the changes affect their meanings.
Only where literary records exist can these changes be traced.

Moreover, since the causes of these changes lie solely in the nation’s mode of apprehension, and very sudden and abrupt transitions are possible in a person’s inner life, languages undergo these transformations, the very ones most decisive for their innermost nature, more rapidly, more frequently and more intensely than they undergo the transformations that come from shifts in meanings themselves as a whole and from the reshaping of sounds.

The study of these changes belongs chiefly to the history of intellectual cultivation. The study of language often leaves them entirely outside its scope and is justified in doing so if it means to confine itself to the material, in a sense coarser, part of language. But it must include them if language is to be presented in the full extent of its relation to the human being, as is the aim here.

sentences.english: β. Stock of Words.
A word is a sound which designates a concept.
There always lies in the word, therefore, unity of sound — which, where sounds are combined, is effected by the accent — and unity of concept.
The simple word is the true individual in language.

For it contains completely the whole act of the understanding performed by language; it is indeed itself the form in which the mind places outside itself again, as such, the Object transformed into its subjectivity (39.); but that which results when it is itself in turn analysed — the syllable and the letter — is no longer language, but only an element of it.
All words, even compound words, are the constituents, the material of discourse, and in the stock of words of a language there therefore lies the entire thought-material of a nation.

The word shares the whole nature of language developed in what precedes; it has the same objectivity and subjectivity (40.), exercises the same power over man (42.), and is equally subject to his freedom (51.); it forms objects into its own ideal world, which in language in general takes the place of the real one (39.).

The distinctive apprehension of things through language lies principally in this, that individual subjectivity, always remaining the same as itself, takes and treats all the constituents of language in the same way, attaching itself to each one; and it derives more from the ideal than from the material part of languages, more from the mode of presentation given through language than from the sounds used in it.

Words which pass, in little-changed tones and designating determinate objects, from generation to generation and from nation to nation can therefore bear this distinctiveness visibly upon them only to a slight extent; it is revealed only in their use and in the way in which they mutually supplement, limit, and determine one another.

Where, therefore, as with the languages of uncultivated nations, this use is known only from scanty specimens of language, mere knowledge of words, incomplete for that very reason, does not suffice to fathom the distinctiveness of the language precisely in its most important aspect.
Editor's note: First publication of this chapter: *Internationale Zeitschrift für allgemeine Sprachwissenschaft* 1, 385—411 (1884).
The number of words possible in a language depends on the number of syllables possible in it (62.a.) and on the special rules and customs governing word-formation in it (62.b.).
It can properly be determined only where it is relatively small and is wholly or for the most part actually exhausted by the language.
This can be the case almost only with languages with monosyllabic words.

Author's note: It is striking that the Chinese language, notwithstanding its poverty in spoken words, does not carry each of the possible words through all the existing modes of accentuation. Still less does it combine all final vowels with every initial consonant.
But if these languages are grouped together as a distinct genus, one must properly understand in what way this is done.
This division cannot be called purely factual.

For a large part of all languages, however polysyllabic they may be, can be traced back by analysis to monosyllabic roots; and if one goes back in thought to the origin of languages, the most natural thing is to assign to the simple concept likewise only a simple sound.
Yet this must not be understood as if every stem-word must necessarily be monosyllabic.

For in our investigation of language, in which we are never able to go back to the beginning, the concept of the stem-word is itself only a relative concept, and any of our languages may have begun with many polysyllabic words alongside monosyllabic ones.

On the other hand, the monosyllabic languages, too, do not possess this property in purity; and when in them two words come together to form a composite concept, it depends only on the accent whether it connects them or, thrusting each forth singly, still separates them.

To decide now whether this separation also holds the concepts further apart in the understanding, or whether the linking of the concepts makes the peculiarity of pronunciation appear only as such, not as a division between words, would probably border on impossibility.

On the other hand, it may well be asserted with good reason that the splitting of the tones, where close combination makes the concepts into one, disturbs the influence which the division of discourse into correct and appropriate word-wholes produces on the mind.
In each individual case it may be indifferent whether the division of sound keeps pace with the division of thought or not.
But in the aggregate the importance is unmistakable, and the thoroughgoing cutting up of the sounds into individual syllables must act disadvantageously on the flow of thoughts.

Meanwhile, investigation has probably never in China itself been directed to these finer mental influences of language; and in nature a disproportion is ordinarily always redressed by other circumstances that intervene alongside it, so that on the whole the same phenomenon emerges again as where it is not present.
Even the concept of monosyllabic languages must therefore be understood with a certain restriction, and the polysyllabic ones may originally have been monosyllabic.

The division into words on which this classification is based rests, even with respect to the sounds, on circumstances which, as has just been shown, are all the more difficult to judge inasmuch as they do not presuppose exact knowledge of the living delivery of discourse.
Nevertheless, the monosyllabic structure of a small number of languages remains a highly remarkable phenomenon which, precisely because of its rarity, deserves the most attentive consideration.
It is entirely false to regard these languages, as though they were child languages, as having stopped at a stage of original imperfection.
The causes of monosyllabicity must certainly be sought in a quite different way and much more deeply.
Since, however, this property is foreign to the American languages, I have wished to assign it its fitting place only here, in the edifice of language in general.
The same holds, in the polysyllabic languages, of the uniformity in the structure of stem-words that is encountered, for example, in the Semitic languages.

Where word-formation is bound to no such fixed form, the number of possible words remains indeterminate, and a multitude of concurring circumstances, of which an account can only rarely be given, determines which of them are actually called into existence.
But it must always be assumed that each one has arisen through another that existed before it.
For all changes in language take place gradually (43.), and what is repeated in speaking is always only what has already been heard, wholly or in part.
The investigation of word-sounds therefore finds itself everywhere in the middle of a chain whose beginning remains inaccessible to it.

There is, however, hardly any need for the cautionary remark that not all languages still in existence need on that account be parts of the same chain, since (46.) there could be different developments of words that have never, or for a long time have not, entered into connection with one another.

Since, however, the sameness of the organs of speech and of their laws makes the same word-sounds, and only a certain number of them, possible everywhere, mere identity or affinity of tone cannot by itself decide (47.) concerning their historical or physiological difference.

Affinity can be conceived in two ways: by derivation, in that the simpler sound becomes, by addition at the end, addition at the beginning, or insertion, the more or less composite one; and by similarity of sound, in that the simple tone sounds again, still simple but changed, or a related idea is designated by a related tone.

From this origin of every word from another word, at most those imitated from sounds of nature might be excepted; they ordinarily pass likewise from generation to generation and from nation to nation, but can also arise suddenly, although even in this case they will always conform to the sound-analogy of the rest of the language.

Here, where only the course of word-formation in a given language is to be investigated, the sole concern is to analyse composite word-sounds into ever simpler ones, as far as this is possible, to develop the analogy of this composition, and in turn to compare the simplest words thus found with one another in their sound-relations.
From this there result, on the one side, the laws and customs of the word-formation of nations and, on the other, the extent, completeness, and archaic character of their word-structure.

To the former belong the alterations of words through the vowel-series, the insertions and alterations of consonants, the extensions of words by sounds placed before and after, repetitions of syllables, and transpositions.
In all this the cruder or finer sense for language of nations can very often be recognized.

The more directly a language has been taken from one already completely formed, the less does it go back up to simple sounds, such as are hardly encountered at all in the stock of words of several of these languages.

Only where considerable tribes have for centuries, in great freedom from foreign mixture, carried their language onward from generation to generation, and its origin is lost in darkness, does that broad and archaic structure appear in which long genealogical series of words can be traced back to their fundamental sounds, these still have meaning in their simplicity, every analogy proves itself in numerous examples, every sound-quality finds beside it several or all of the others situated in the same sphere or genus, and in which consequently strict analogy guides the mind through a comprehensive system of word-sounds.

This now reacts upon the nation, in addition to the influence of such fullness and regularity on use, also in itself, in clear consciousness as in obscure feeling; and the production of language in it becomes more fruitful for everything with which it stands in contact, when a world of tones that orders itself easily and wonderfully takes its place beside the world of ideas.

The structure of such a language links every individual to far more distant times, to a far more original state of the human race, to a mass, appearing infinite, of thoughts and sensations that have once existed and yet always in some way touch and recall one another.
Herein lies (55.) the system of rules of word-formation, which, even in the merely lexical comparison of languages, must be distinguished from the tones themselves.
Its basis is the sound-system.

For the finer and more intellectual the hearing and the sense for language prove themselves to be in this system, the more carefully is every modification of the tone — arising perhaps at first only by chance, through insertion of a breath, a vowel, a nasal sound — attended to and carried through in similar cases, and the more analogically are other changes of the same kind formed after it.

From related nations the fundamental features of this system pass over into related languages, and the sameness of kind of languages can in many respects be recognized more correctly from lexical analogy than from grammatical analogy.
For it does not rest, as the latter does, on general laws of thought, but attaches itself immediately to the tone.
The more individual a sameness of kind is, however, the more surely it points to a historical connection.

Care must, however, be taken to note the cases where words in whose structure analogies of this kind are indicated have passed into other languages without these analogies themselves — that is, without the feeling for them in the other nation, and therefore without further development by it — and now become parts of a language in which no such structure exists in such perfection, or in which a different system of it exists.

From this inner connection of words, in their sounds also, it now follows of itself that the words of several languages must not be compared immediately with one another for the purpose of discovering their sameness of kind, but that a comparison of them in each language separately must first precede.
The alphabetical placing side by side of the words of different languages tears each of these languages out of its natural context.

But when the comparison of the words of one language with one another has been made, two objects result for comparison with another language: the rules of lexical analogy and the fundamental sounds, and, together with the former, the composite words that have passed from one language into the other and are actually formed according to these rules.
A comparison that carries its guarantee in itself can be made only in this way.

But if, as very often happens, from lack of aids, or because a language has no inner structure executed in so intelligible a manner, and because even that which exists is never known quite completely, one is thrown back on immediate comparison of words, the two words to be compared must nevertheless first be investigated as exactly as possible, each in its own language, as to their origin, so as not to regard words that are really different as of the same kind on account of merely apparent similarity of sound.

Author's note: Thus one might regard Coptic *hrosch* and Sanskrit *rôsha*, which both mean ‘anger’, as of the same kind, since the *h* here could be a mere aspiration of the *r*, just as *hloili* is also *loili*. More careful comparison, however, shows that *hrosch* arose from *horsch*, with the same meaning, as *hroyr* arose from *hoyrooy* and *heri*, and that that similarity of sound with the Indian word is therefore merely accidental.

In all the relations considered here, attention has been paid only to the dependence of word-formation on the nation's treatment of tone, to the way in which it gives extent and manifoldness to the stock of its word-sounds.

But regard for meaning is also principally associated with word-formation; and if, for example, the origin of *λαμβάνω* from *λάβω* is mere alteration of tone, that of *legen* from *liegen* carries with it a nuance of sense.

Word-formation by composition rests wholly on meaning; in it several concepts are always combined, either into a new third concept or, as in formation by prefixes and suffixes, merely for the different determination of the principal concept.
The sound-relations cooperate in this only occasionally and in a subordinate way.

In the choice of sounds for concepts, language naturally allows itself to be guided by the clearer and obscurer relations which feeling and imagination, in accordance with the individuality of nations, find among them.

Historically, however, this is lost in the times of the invention of language, which no investigation can any longer reach; and through gradual alteration of language, in which now the tone is gradually deflected further from the fundamental tone, now the concept from the fundamental concept, this relation between tone and meaning very often undergoes a complete alteration.

Moreover, the feeling, by its nature more indeterminate, on which it rests, is different in different peoples; and precisely those nations which possess more original languages — that is, languages bearing fewer traces of great upheavals — tolerate fewer colliding consonants in their syllables, and consequently are without one more means of determining the character of the word-sound.

It is therefore a by no means unusual phenomenon to see strong and even repugnant concepts paired with gentle and soft sounds, and vice versa; and in historical investigations of language no weight at all is to be placed on this analogy.
Fantasy and acumen find in this a wide but highly uncertain field; and for ten examples proving such agreement of tone with meaning, one comes upon a far greater number in which it is absent.
On the other hand, it would be equally incorrect to turn attention wholly away from it.
For it cannot be denied that in languages of great age and of broad and manifold word-structure the feeling of such an unmistakable agreement presents itself more frequently than in others.

But where it continues to act for centuries in a mother tongue that has remained unmixed, upon the same nation, it heightens and strengthens the influence of language, in which everything depends on making the word, through the closest fusion of tone with concept, into a distinctive being hovering between man and the world, at once dependent on and independent of both.
This is especially visible in German and in the languages dependent on it.

Word-sounds do indeed pass, together with their meanings, from generation to generation and from tribe to tribe; but since the concept is more mobile than the sensibly perceptible sound, and forms easier transitions according to relations that lie now in it, now in the individual, now also in external circumstances, deflections of meanings arise more frequently than deflections of tone.

One may therefore regard word-sounds as forms that have preserved themselves down to us from hoary antiquity, and have preserved within themselves a more or less changing content, through which, however, there always winds a thread, albeit often only a loosely connecting one.
Already in this respect there becomes necessary, in the investigation of linguistic structure, a separation of the word as sound and as concept, a separation that admittedly does not exist in nature.

For the continuous series of presentations requires, just as does the continuous series of tones, division into units of thought corresponding to the word-sounds, through which ideal Objects can be apprehended and connected.

To each such unit of thought, and consequently to every word, there corresponds an object, either one that can be pointed out corporeally in nature, or one formed by the mind, more or less independently of sensible perception.

For although in this latter case the word itself is this object, one must distinguish the word in general and in itself from the word thought at a determinate moment by a determinate individual, just as one must in the same way distinguish the language as a whole.
The word causes the soul to present to itself the object given in the word.

This presentation must be distinguished from the object; it can be individually different, and must be so, since it is determined on all sides, whereas the object, as Object, can only ever be grasped more generally; besides the objective part, which refers to the object, it has a subjective part, lying in the mode of apprehension, both in the intellectual view and in the sensation accompanying it.

But again, it hardly needs remarking that this separation rests only on abstraction, that the word can have no place outside thinking, and just as little can its object, if the latter is an incorporeal one, that the word itself is each time produced wholly by the mind, that it truly has its completeness and individuality only in the thinking of the moment, and as a constituent of language, as an Object of linguistic investigation, is only a general form, individualizable in different ways, though in ways limited by its nature.
This remains the case also with sensible objects, since it is never they directly, but always only that presentation of them which the word gives of them, that becomes present to the soul.

On the fact that every word of a language possesses a certain latitude for the possibility of different kinds of presentations rests the possibility that, in one and the same language, the modes of presentation of quite different human individualities and ages can unite, and that, despite the sameness of the general language, each person (50.) can nevertheless have his own.

For understanding is not a meeting of modes of presentation in an indivisible point, but a meeting of spheres of thought, of which the more general part coincides, the more individual projects beyond it.

Through this the mental progress of the human race becomes possible, in that every enlargement of thinking that has been won can pass into the possession of others without laying fetters in them on the freedom that is necessary for appropriation and for new enlargement, and in that at the same time the forms of thinking, the languages, undergo the changes prescribed for them, as for everything bound to earthly appearance, in their course of development.

In every meaning of a word, therefore, attention is to be directed to how it leaves the individual mode of presentation free and how it determines it, and a history of words and of their individual meanings can be carried through all the different ways in which they have been taken and used.

The concept raised to the clarity and determinateness of the word is in every case the result of the co-operation of the whole power of the soul, and since it is now the peculiarity of the word to call forth this concept through the tone, as through an electric shock, its effect radiates through the whole soul in all directions.

The unity of a power cannot be split into parts, yet in the formation and influence of the word three great and principal relations do stand out, under which every word can be considered and tested: its logical construction, its sensible validity, and its impression on feeling.

Each of these three items, however, appears again in the word in a twofold way, since one must distinguish the presentation of the object itself (85.) from that which the word, according to its formation and origin, gives of it, and of these two presentations neither cancels the other, but both enter into a certain relation to one another.
The word gives the concept shape, and through the tone, immediately before the ear, and mediately before all the sensible powers of the soul, sensible validity.

The word grasps every concept as a general one, designates, strictly taken, always classes of reality, even when it is a proper name, since it then comprehends together all the states of what is designated, different in time and space (presenting it as a class in which it is contained in all these states just as different individuals are contained in a generic concept).
But it makes itself, and consequently also the concept contained in it, into an individual of language.

It can therefore take that concept only from a single standpoint, yet it must give up nothing of its content, and this is achieved in that the word imparts to the soul, in the directions of those three principal relations, a determinate excitation, through which the generation of the concept does indeed take place completely, but from a sharply determinate side.

Through this there arise, in the words of several languages that have the same meaning, different presentations of the same object, and this constitution of the word contributes principally to each language affording a world-view of its own.
Just as language, and in it the word, generalizes the individual nature of the world, so it spiritualizes the material-like nature of that world in outer and inner perception.
But just as the word itself in turn becomes an individual in language, so it also becomes corporeal in it by taking on tone, and serves the mind as material for new activity.

The one and the other, however, happen at the same time and in indivisible unity, synthetically, and generality and individuality, spirituality and materiality interpenetrate one another in the word, which, since those concepts would otherwise cancel one another, is possible only through the fact that the word, thought as a constituent of language outside the soul, is nothing but an excitation to thinking, thought as a completed concept in the soul, is thinking itself, and that this unceasing developing and returning of the general and non-sensible out of the individual and sensible, and back into the same, belongs peculiarly to human mental power.

If we now look back at the three principal directions mentioned above (87.), in which the word excites the soul, the word can possess sensible validity and validity for sensation only in so far as it can preserve the same for itself in the domain of intellectuality.

This happens, however, only in that this content of sense and feeling is at the same time, and again synthetically, destroyed as material and preserved as form, which is the work of the imagination, the mediatress of the opposed natures in mankind.

Since now the intellectual content of the word, too, can unite with the sensible content only in its domain, this domain is properly the sphere in which the word hovers, in that the imagination gathers together the total powers of the soul for producing or understanding it.

The way in which the word, always in those three directions, brings the objects of outer and inner perception before the soul may be called the Objective in it, its matter, but the way in which the faculties of the soul, in those directions, enter into relation to one another and fuse into the unity of co-operation may be called the Subjective in it, its form.

Both lie undeniably in language and in every single one of its words; in that they were the individuality of the speakers, they have attached themselves to the sounds, and through them return into living individuality.

For the wonderful kind of embodiment of a mental generation, which brings forth a like generation in the other, is indeed the truly peculiar nature of language, and rests pre-eminently on its principal constituent, the word.
Form, however, is still more important than matter.

For it is attached to the language as a whole, and if therefore the language is apprehended, even as dead or foreign, by a very different individuality, it nevertheless compels that individuality to adopt its mode of intuition, in that it ensnares it with that mode on all sides.

Matter not only cannot do this, but the particular mode of presenting the object does not even always remain recognizable in the word, or at least is no longer felt as it was at its origin; the individuality of the word is lost in the generality of the concept.
I have already pointed to this above (87.) in the distinction between the presentation of the object and the word's presentation of it.

This distinction admittedly becomes possible only through the fact that the word, as embodied concept, is gradually adapted by very different individualities to different modes of intuition, in which the use of the moment does not present the object at all as the first inventor did; but understood in this way, whole series of examples of it can be shown.

The expressions for corporeal objects have certainly for the most part arisen from properties that were pre-eminently striking in them, and are nothing other than substantives that have become adjectives; non-sensible concepts are metaphorically designated after corporeal ones, grammatical concepts, which merely determine the connexion of speech, after words for thing-concepts.
In all these cases the character of the original designation very often, indeed for the most part, perishes, and the concept of the object, taken generally or in another way, steps into its place.

Hardly was the property of drinking doubly, through the trunk and the mouth, always thought of with the Indian *dwîpa* for 'elephant'; few who use the German *Vernunft* and *zurück* think of the fact that the former comes from *vernehmen*, the latter from *Rücken*.
Many words that formerly had no such subsidiary meaning at all are later used only in a joking, ironic or contemptuous way.

Thus the matter of the word changes; even between the same tone and the same object designated by it, the mind finds a play-room of comfortable latitude for inserting differently nuanced kinds of presentation; properly, however, under the same acoustic sound a different word is uttered each time.
For only what is actually thought or spoken is the word proper; what inherits itself on, as it were dead, in language is only the husk, enlivened ever again, and ever somewhat differently.
In what is thought or spoken, matter and form are in every case determined together by the character of the word and of the language and by that of the speaker.
This coincides with what was remarked above (86.), that the nature of the word, even in the same language, allows the individual to have, up to a certain degree, a language of his own.
It is, however, different therein, that that takes place even where the matter and form of the word-sound are completely felt, whereas here the opposite case is being spoken of.
Here, therefore, a twofold latitude of the sound-form, as husk of the concept, reveals itself.
If in the words of a language the original mode of intuiting objects gradually becomes effaced, it is not to be denied that a certain individuality and sensible liveliness perishes in it.
But it is not on that account to be said that it does not perhaps gain thereby on the other side.
For the merits of languages are not determined by the partial wealth of images and concepts that they supply to the soul, but by their effect on thinking and feeling in general.

Thus, for example, the designation of objects by their properties, cited at (90.), affords, so long as it is alive in a language, greater fullness of intuition, but it also has, not to mention other lesser ones, the disadvantage that it restricts too one-sidedly the freedom in presenting the object, and, forming substantives too visibly from adjectives, disturbs the agreement in which language, following nature also in its form, must, for the expression of independent beings, use in that form words also endowed with independence.

Much more appropriately acts the agreement of the concept with the sound according to an obscure feeling of kinship (83.), since the soul is thereby attuned and guided, but not restricted in the manner of presentation.

If linguistic investigation directs itself to these relations, seeks them out in the words without putting them into them, and in this way awakens the linguistic sense of the nation, which is always akin, even unconsciously, to the mother tongue, and thereby effects clearer insight and a finer feeling for the language, then the original individuality of the words can step forth again more brightly into the light, and now subordinates itself, without doing further harm, to the apprehension of objects that has in the course of time become freer and more intellectual.
Two languages will not easily keep, in the form of their words, a perfect equilibrium among the different excitations that the soul experiences through them.

One of these excitations will predominate over another, and the force will also be different with which — and on this the clarity and determinateness of thinking pre-eminently rest — these excitations strike together in the concept into the presentation of the object.
Investigations of this kind can be made only on highly cultivated languages, but mere feeling, too, perceives the differences.
In one there reigns a greater sensible clarity, another attunes feeling more, a third contents itself more drily with logical determination.
The changing direction of the nation can alter this character, but, incessantly subject to its influences, can never abandon it.
It also partly determines the use that is made of the language, the more poetic, philosophical, scientific character of its literature, and is in turn determined by the latter.

With the matter of words there now comes in addition the nature of the objects, and there thus arise, with every word, the questions: what does the word comprehend together as its object? how does it designate what is thus comprehended together? and what subsidiary concept, according to accompanying feeling, does it connect with this designation?

If these questions are put in succession from a twofold standpoint, first from that of one language with respect to the manifoldness of objects, then from the standpoint of the latter with respect to the words of several languages, the relation of the designation to what is designated will be exhausted, at least as to direction.
Language, namely, proceeds in word-formation in a uniform way, and it is this way that must be investigated through the examination of a considerable number of words.
The material content of words seems to be determined of itself by the objects of thinking.

Comparative investigation of several languages, however, shows the opposite, and since the word depends not immediately on the object but on the apprehension of it, indeed many objects are only first formed by the soul, it must necessarily be so.

The first law prevailing here is now that of a correct division of the thought-material by language, or, expressed otherwise, that the object of the word should be circumscribed by firm boundaries, should contain everything that belongs to the completion of its concept, and nothing that is not essential to it but only attaches to it accidentally.

Even with expressions for corporeal objects, their meanings are not always appropriate to the firm boundaries in nature, but waver about among them; this indeterminateness is found still more frequently with intellectual designations; and it is quite usual, in the languages with which we are here immediately concerned, to find determinations mixed in with the concept that disturb its generality and that it must carry about with it only to the detriment of distinctness.
On the other hand, however, there are also in several languages new and excellently formed concepts, which must count as genuine enlargements of thinking.

For the possession of a word for a concept not hitherto thought within these boundaries is of immeasurable gain, when it concerns a mass of thought-material that can intervene in thinking so as to promote the winning of enlarged views.

In this distribution of concepts over words there is now revealed, in the first instance, the nation's sense for correct and sharp apprehension of nature and for logical exactness; but in higher respects there emerges from it the fortunate creative capacity of the mind.

Certainly, however, one must picture this to oneself only very rarely as if a new word were given to a purely thought concept; ordinarily only a word hitherto taken in a lower or more indeterminate meaning is re-stamped.
Of this kind in Sanskrit are *kaṭi*, *taṭa*, *śrôṇi*, *nitamba*, which all indicate the region of the body around the hips within an indeterminate delimitation.
One may adduce here the Sanskrit *nyâya* and *yôga*.
The second law with respect to the content of words is that the word should not comprehend in itself too many meanings, and meanings connected with one another by too loose bonds of kinship.
This is found in some languages more than in others; complaint is made of it in particular in Chinese and Sanskrit.

Yet one should not forget that this complaint mostly hits only the defectiveness of dictionaries, which, without order and reflection, let all the meanings in which the word is found in individual passages follow one upon another, and from every passage single out precisely the most determinate meaning to which the connexion of the concepts constrains the natural and simple sense of the word over.
If this were duly appreciated, and the periods and kinds of use were distinguished, that ambiguity, which at present admittedly disturbs the beginner in particular, would melt down a great deal.

Where it cannot, however, be denied, it coincides on the one side with the indeterminateness censured above (96.), which allows more than one determination of the concept, and consequently several concepts, but on the other side it can also arise from too ingenious a spinning-out of a concept into all the threads issuing from it, or from a predilection for all too bold metaphors, and consequently be peculiar precisely to the languages of very ingenious nations.
With the ambiguity of words, however, one must not confuse the widely comprehending scope of their meaning.

With the latter, the meaning nonetheless remains simple, and a language that truly promotes reflection must precisely have fixed thought even at the highest levels of abstraction, or the lowest of individualizing determination (since such words can arise at both).

Only the manifoldness of concrete meanings standing side by side, and the arbitrary application of general meanings to one of the many things comprehended under them, disturbs the determinateness of expression and ease of intelligibility.

By the mode of designating the concept in the word I do not here understand designation through tone, although the designation of which we are speaking here determines tone, and sometimes coincides with it.
Otherwise, however, tone in general (73–82.) and especially in relation to meaning (83.) has already been spoken of above.
Here what is at issue is the content of the word, that is, the concept.

But the concept can be given neither in its definition nor, if it belongs to a corporeal object, in the whole being of the latter; the word must shape it in unity (88.); that, therefore, through which it indicates it to the mind of the hearer is, even as concept, its designation.

Originally this designation (which properly is such only in relation to the hearer, but on the speaker's part is an apprehension) lies in every word: in those formed after natural sounds, in the sounding of the objects, in others for corporeal things in other of their properties, in intellectual ones in the metaphors chosen to indicate them.

For in that the concept was clothed in a tone, the tongue had after all to let itself be determined by something in the choice of that tone, and this could only be this mode of intuition, comprehending the whole concept together in one point.

This mode itself, however, one can only think of as sensible, partly because it is to guide the choice of tone, partly because the whole of word-formation (89.) hovers in the sphere of the imagination.

In most cases, however, this sensible mode of apprehending the object, which preceded the tone, or arose simultaneously with it, yet always determining it, is no longer to be traced, and then it still hangs merely on the effect exercised on the tone, sometimes not even any longer on this in a recognizable way.

In the former case the sound-character of the word (its hardness or softness, its brightness or dullness, and so forth), in the latter merely the acoustic sound of the articulated tones themselves, is the designation of the word-content.
Examples are given by the three German words: *Fliege*, *Krähe*, *Gans*.

In the first, the designation of the concept is the incessantly recurring flying, whereby the animal becomes so pre-eminently troublesome; in the second, the cry of the bird; in the third, the mere word, stemming from Indian, and not explicable even there.
Similar examples are afforded by the words for mental concepts with and without recognizable metaphors.
This mode of designating the concept might be called the self-meaning of words.
For through it they really distinguish themselves from others devoted to the same object.

It is important in many respects to investigate whether in a language such a self-meaning is peculiar to many words, and also to distinguish the case already indicated at (91.), whether it is still generally felt by the people, or now lies there recognizable only to the investigator.
Since the predominance of self-meanings must rightly be regarded as what is more original in languages, conclusions can be drawn from it as to the changes that have taken place in the language.

But they themselves, in so far as they reveal themselves with reliability, are important to investigate, because they show the direction in which a people has apprehended nature, and has appropriated what is mental to language in a sensible covering.

But since one is here supposed to be on historical ground, one must be careful not to concede too much to ingenuity and imagination in this, and to restrict oneself only to that to which sure traces of the formation lead.

The sensible material of the word, of which we are speaking here, is the handle by which the mind grasps intellectual concepts, and if one wishes to remain true to the course of nature, one must think of their designation in language not as descending from concept to designation, but, conversely, as ascending up to it.

It is everywhere in mankind as follows: out of appearances that step into existence, as it were accidentally, through the mere fruitfulness of generating powers, a whole builds itself up, out of which afterwards the unity of an idea radiates towards the observing mind, and it is no different in language.

In the colourful manifoldness of tones which the perception of nature, the need of communication, and social talkativeness entice forth, the soul discovers — and the more frequently and the more full of genius, the more higher intellectual power and finer linguistic sense is present in it itself — the mental relations, and stamps out the words that are present in meanings corresponding to them.

Not through a sort of dull brooding over the idea-material, occupied with dividing and dissecting, but through the fertilization of the natural mass of tones by a lively mind, always directed towards what is higher, there arises in languages a rich and deep idea-content in words ingeniously appropriated to it.
The word, as designation of the concept, is akin to the sign and to the symbol.

Here, however, is the place to fix these three concepts exactly, and to show that the word does indeed share properties with the other two, but, according to its innermost nature, is different from both.

In so far as it calls forth the concept through its sound, it admittedly fulfils the purpose of a sign, but it steps wholly out of the class of signs through the fact that what is designated has an existence independent of its sign, whereas the concept only first receives its completion through the word, and the two cannot be separated from one another.
To misconceive this, and to regard words as mere signs, is the fundamental error that destroys all science of language and all correct appreciation of language.
In so far as the word transforms the concept into a sensible material before the imagination, it resembles the symbol.

For it foists a shape upon the idea, and in the case of the corporeal object it abstracts from the totality of its reality, in that it holds it fast at one characteristic mark, and in this mark designates it through something foreign to it, a tone.
The sound thus, in this way like a hieroglyph, encloses the concept within itself.

In the symbol, the sensible and the non-sensible, mutually interpenetrating one another, are regarded as one, the latter revealing itself in the former, the former expanding itself to the latter; idea and corporeal material coincide.

With the word, too, the concept cannot be purely separated off from the sound: not in itself, since it cannot be thought without language; not from the sound peculiar determinately to it in a language, because it at the same time bears the latter's individuality upon itself.
Nevertheless the word is thoroughly different from the symbol.

The latter demands a complete natural form, subsisting for itself, which can also be considered without any relation to a indwelling idea, but from which, as soon as it shows itself as symbol, the idea radiates forth from all its parts.

The sound in the word (as the word's sensible material, corresponding to that natural form), by contrast, is nothing without relation to the concept, since it has exclusively the determination to call the latter forth in shaped form.

It is therefore a quite different coinciding of the sensible and the non-sensible in symbol and in word; in the latter, sound and concept, without even admitting a separation, and each incomplete for itself, are one and make up one being, but the sound in a certain measure yields to the concept, which it is only to call forth and to shape.

In the symbol the natural form is independent at the same time as the idea interpenetrating it, and maintains its rights pre-eminently; both are the same, since from every point of the one the other radiates forth, but they are not one.
The natural form remains, even without an idea thought in it, in everything through which it counted in the symbol, like the body when the soul leaves it.

Words and word-sounds, however, like all other objects, can be treated as symbols in their constitution and number and in connexion with their meaning, and so it is presumably to be understood when it is related of the Egyptian priests that they celebrated the gods through the sounding-forth, strung one after another, of the seven vowels.
