The symbol expressly demands the fusion of the non-sensible with the sensible; the body is not to be merely body, the idea not merely idea.

Language, by contrast, is a purely mental striving, going (24.) from thinking to thinking, only on this path compelled to take on corporeal material, and only as little as possible, only the light tone that dies away at once, and of this only the articulated tone, the tone reduced, with the greatest possible cutting-away of all noise, to a merely audible relation.
The symbolizing understanding and the sense and genius for language therefore stand in natural opposition to one another.
They also accustom the mind to a quite different tarrying in the succession of presentations, which is one of the most principal points in the formation of minds in individuals and nations.

Symbolizing leads to deepening oneself in the individual object, whose shell must as it were be penetrated in order to perceive the idea radiating through it; linguistic sense carries the mind away in irresistibly living movement.
For it follows the fugitivity of thought and strives after its infinity.

Since every word belongs to a series, and none completely exhausts its concept, it passes over from one to another, and runs through the succession of thoughts developing little by little, leaving behind it only the lightest incisions, those that disturb the interrupted connexion least through pauses.

Where the obscure feeling of the constitution of the object is laid into the tone of the word, as in *Stärke* firmness, in *Wolke*, *Wolle*, *Wald* the wavering indeterminateness of delimitation and of the coming-together of the parts before the eye, there there does in fact lie something symbolic in it.
For this constitution then shines forth from the tone, and the latter acts like an image of it on feeling.
But the word-sound itself can nonetheless not on that account be called a symbol.
For its meaning, on which this its symbolic part only co-operates, is not recognized from it, but on the quite different path which language in general takes.
Still more determinately and more frequently, what is symbolic lies in the concept of words, and precisely in that of which we are speaking here, their sensible designation.
This is the case with all metaphorical expressions.
But this, too, does not alter the nature of the word.

This undeniable symbolizing of language proves that the fortunate disposition for it beneficially supports linguistic sense, but now it also becomes fully clear in what relation the two stand to one another.

Gift and urge must be present to seek out the sensible and the non-sensible in one another and to wrap the one in the other, but the bright and clear direction towards what is mental must predominate, and through the living strength of the power of thought suppress the inclination to tarry precisely with the obscure and mysterious connexion of the two.

Since what is at issue here is the sensible presentation lying in the word and its self-meaning, the question arises: what, properly, does the soul sensibly present to itself with the word? the object as a whole? or the properties apprehended in it in the word? or something indeterminate corresponding to the feeling excited through the word? or, in peoples that have long possessed an alphabet, the written characters?
To investigate this through self-observation would probably be difficult.
The intention alone already alters the object of observation, and certainly the presentation itself, too, changes according to individuality and circumstances through all those cases.

What, by contrast, must be held fast not only as certain but also as decisive for recognizing the true nature of language is that the word never brings the object into presentation otherwise, and never lets the latter tarry with it longer, than the connexion of thoughts of the moment requires — the connexion to which it subordinates it and into which it interweaves it as a member.

This lies in the nature of the word, which indeed puts tones in the place of real objects only in order, through this mediation, to transform the latter into thoughts; it lies further in the fact that the series of thoughts expressed through several words is, strictly taken,
one, and speech is a whole, in which the incisions always at the same time have the purpose of making the structure, as a whole, pre-eminently visible.
It is therefore one of the most important properties of the word to excite in presentation precisely that, and no more, than use requires.
This is indeed effected for the most part through the appropriate connexion with other determining words and through the whole direction given to the hearer's soul.

But it lies in part also in the formation of the word, which in this respect must possess purity, sharpness, sobriety in the determination of the concept, and full appropriateness to a clearly thought purpose.

From this there arises at the same time the necessity of several expressions for the same object according to the difference of use, in different indication of the sides singled out in it, and in different moods of soul.
For these, too, come into consideration here alongside the logical purpose of speech, and act pre-eminently on the kind of sensible presentation lying in the word.
For the same word is manifestly accompanied by different ones in a poetic delivery and in a scientific one.

Here, too, however, language creates more accidentally than intentionally, and the words akin in sense are often only words transferred from other dialects with the subsidiary concept taken up in them there.

The accompanying feeling (95.) acts on words either as an individual sensation of the mind [*Gemüth*], or as a total attunement of the combined intellectual powers and powers of the mind [*Gemüthskräfte*], in which the former do indeed rule, but take on the colour of the latter.

From the former arise the caressing, honouring, solemn, scolding, contemptuous, mocking, joking expressions, from the latter the poetic, philosophical, exhortingly moving expressions, and so forth. Properly no word is uttered without one of these nuances of sensation, even if imperceptible in the individual case, since the strings struck thereby always lie there tensed in the mind [*Gemüth*].

Here, however, only those particular words are at issue into whose formation these determinations of feeling have so passed over that they now always excite the same determinations, and cannot be used where these are not in their place.
In individual languages one perceives in these expressions a twofold remarkable appearance.
The languages of uncultivated peoples contain a great number of such expressions as betray individual sensation of the mind [*Gemüth*].

Language always spiritualizes man, leads him up first to pure intellectuality, but then, if no counterweight intervenes, over beyond the summit-point to a dry, sophistical and playful one; but it does this only gradually.
All popular dialects make more frequent use of caressing, diminutive, augmentative, pejorative words than the higher, purified dialect does.
On the other hand, one must not look there for particular poetic words; everything is still in a certain measure poetic, and is taken up as such without consciousness of the opposite.
In the languages of some highly cultivated nations, on the other side, this consciousness is so fine and lively, and delivery so chaste, that a poetic word is never tolerated in unfettered speech.

This springs only mediately from the poetic feeling of the nation, but immediately from the feeling for prose as a kind of speech of its own, a feeling presupposing a much more highly raised and more finely purified linguistic sense.
One therefore finds this only in the noblest languages, and those worked on with the most mind.

With philosophical words one must distinguish the merely logical ones, constructed by the understanding, which belong only to the technical-scientific, from those that have arisen, through synthesizing reason, from deeper reflection or higher revelation.
Where, as in Indian, abstract philosophy has entered into a grand connexion with the highest poetry, these expressions are found in pre-eminent strength and beauty.
In what has gone before I have tried to analyse the nature and requirements of words, each considered singly by itself, in order to show how language designates the individual concept.

It is now necessary to examine the whole stock of the words of one language in the relations of their meaning to one another, and in relation to the extent of objects and concepts, in order to show how language proceeds to create fitting expressions for every use in speech, and to designate the whole mass of concepts that occur.
Every language, whatever it may be, bears in its bosom at every moment of its existence the expression of all concepts that can ever develop in the nation.
Every language, moreover, at the particular moment of its life in question, is exactly equal to the particular extent of thought of the nation at that moment.

Every language, finally, in each of its states forms the whole of a view of the world, in that it contains expression for all presentations which the nation forms of the world, and for all sensations which the world produces in it.
These propositions rest on the identity of thinking and speaking.
What man can think, that he is also able to say.

The thinking of a nation sometimes develops through mixture with another, in which case language too receives foreign increment, but it can also form itself wholly out of itself, and complete its whole course within itself, and nation and language thrive better and more peculiarly thereby, if it succeeds.
The thinking of the nation, consisting of the thinking of each individual, must at every moment be a whole.

For it is the way in which man at every moment asserts his mental existence in its position in relation to the world, and since this whole existence, which consists only in this activity, necessarily contracts itself into each individual act of thinking; this cannot happen partially, not in mutilated fashion.
Those propositions are, however, of the highest importance for the correct appreciation of language.

For it rests upon them that one regards language at no moment of its life as closed off, but always as advancing, everything contained in it as a germ of new development, and regards its advance not mechanically, as an attaching of parts, but truly organically, as an unfolding of a whole out of a whole.

The possibility of this nature of language lies in what has already been spoken of above, in the capacity of articulated sounds for transpositions and combinations of all kinds, whereby, through production of small differences while general similarity remains, whole families of word-sounds (79.) arise from one basic sound, and through the deflection of the same word to kindred meanings, through the fixing of words generally synonymous, and through the new stamping of words otherwise used differently.
It is a creating of sounds and a creating of concepts through which language grows within itself; the latter goes on to infinity, but the former has, as all experience shows, a limit.
Language reaches a point where the richness of sounds is no longer increased from its own bosom, but at most still through the taking up of foreign words.
Further working then becomes in a certain measure more inward, and restricts itself to the fixing and modifying of meanings.
The lack of all historical experience forbids saying anything more precise about this dividing point.
So much, however, one does see, that it lies where the coming together and mingling of tribes with one another ceases, either itself or in its effect upon language.

For all inner enlargement of language in its sounds can after all be suitably conceived only on the supposition that several persons speaking the same language, through peculiarity or separation, bring differences into it which then pass into the whole, already accompanied by differences of meaning too, or only receiving them there.

Through the fact that everyone properly, in order to be understood, wants to speak as the other does, but everyone nevertheless, because he is after all physically and mentally another, really speaks somewhat differently, but this something different is nevertheless understood and taken up again, a great manifoldness of word-sounds can arise in a language, if one conceives this as continuing for centuries among individuals, families and tribes.
That one dialect enriches another and the general language, we indeed often experience ourselves.
Insofar as by the richness of a language one understands its capacity to satisfy the need for expression, one can call all languages equally rich.
For as soon as one truly possesses a language, no concept and no turn of ideas can lack the appropriate designation.

That is not to say, however, that examination of the richness of a language is an idle inquiry, if only one understands rightly the sense of the expression, and there are indeed different degrees and kinds of it.

First it is a question of every object or concept that sets itself apart distinctly as an individual one also finding in the language an individual word designating it without circumlocution; as, secondly, of objects likewise not lacking the due diversity of expression according to the sensation with which one speaks, and the mode of intuition towards which one is working.
But there can also, thirdly, be several words for the same object, without noticeable difference of meaning or intention, and, fourthly and finally, several forms of the same word.
It is the case in all languages that what some express by a single word is circumlocuted by others with several, and the clarity and determinateness of the designation can nevertheless be the same.
Yet it is by no means indifferent when a language must often have recourse to circumlocution.
The communication of thoughts, the immediate purpose of speech, admittedly does not suffer thereby; but the difference lies in the form of language, its reaction upon thinking in general.

For one must never forget that the character of language, as an instrument of thinking, exerts an immediate influence upon thinking, raises or lowers its clarity, determinateness, rapidity and sharpness, gives it a sensuous direction outwards or a mental direction inwards, and that this is by far the most important side in it.

Where now every concept finds its word appointed for it, there this richness stirs the mind; language appears like the world, in which object too presses upon object, and as a view of the world it is after all to place itself between nature and man.

I shall also return later to the point that it is of the highest importance that language, abandoning the barren abstractedness of thoughts, should take up into its form the form of external actuality.
This is proved here too.

Even a language poor in words can express a multitude of concepts and series of ideas, even with clarity and determinateness; one sees an example of this in the meagre use which some mission writings make of non-European languages certainly richer in themselves.
The content of the thought is then indeed satisfied.
But the poverty of the language drags the mind down, and thinking in such representation lacks fullness, freshness and liveliness.
For the same reasons, several words for the same concept, even if they offered scarcely noticeable differences, and several forms of the same word, must also not appear as a superfluous luxury.

They not only increase the sensuous fullness of language, but also give opportunity, in the advancing mental development of the nation, to nuance concepts more finely and to determine them more exactly, at least through the use of the different expressions, even if it cannot always be shown in the dictionary.

Even when languages, like English, having flowed together from different ones, possess for certain concepts two expressions different merely in their origin, such as *freedom* and *liberty*, the use of them by speakers of fine sense and linguistic knowledge is nevertheless not wholly indifferent.
In general no kind of richness of languages is to be slighted.

Each proves that, whether it is to be ascribed to the duration of their existence, to the multitude of tribes and individuals who spoke them, or to the mental activity of the nation, much speaking in manifold ways went on in it, and consequently many thoughts and sensations passed into it.
But the more content of human existence sounds back towards the mind from a language, the greater, livelier and more mental is its stimulating power.

In order to judge completely the character of a language with respect to its stock of words, one would have to compare this stock with the mass of possible concepts, what is designated with what is to be designated.

Understood of pure concepts, this is impossible, since the material of thought cannot be purely separated from the material of language; rather designation first completes the arising, before the mind, of what is to be designated.
Even with objects of nature this is the case, since the word after all designates not them in general, but the view of them grounded in the language.
Yet this concerns only strict and wholly exact analysis; otherwise one can indeed ask, what finds in a given language expressions originally peculiar to it?
But with non-sensuous concepts this separation of word and concept is in part much less, in part not at all, to be attempted.
There is, however, an analogue by means of which one can at least to some extent attain the intended purpose.

One can namely put in place of the concepts to be thought purely those actually designated in a number of languages, and measure the mass of what admits and requires designation by what is usually designated, as the case may be, in the various known languages.
Insofar the study of existing languages serves to test the extent of thinking and feeling that has actually existed in the human race.

If one now combines this method with investigation of the pure material of thought, separated from any particular language, by means of setting up general categories of objects and concepts, and division descending ever further, but with the constant consciousness that, where in this descent one comes to the individual concept, a particular language must enter, one can, without falling into errors, nevertheless hold together the material of thought to be designated, not purely and completely, but sufficiently for linguistic inquiry, with the stock of words of a language.

Dictionaries ordered by categories, such as Pollux and Amara's *Cosha*, are useful aids for this, and it was a purposeful idea of Havestadt's also to order the words of the language of Chile in this way.

But these works must be very much completed, and one should not omit to bring together from as many languages as it is possible to compare the words by which objects are designated, or concepts stamped, which in other languages find no exhaustive expression in a word of their own.
I must indeed repeat here that, if one takes it sharply and exactly, no word of one language corresponds completely to that of another.
Here, however, only those cases are in question where through a word, for those who did not previously know the language, a really new concept, or a new important nuance of a concept, arises.

For what is at issue here is the discovery of the material of thought to be designated, and for this mere advance by categories and logical definitions cannot suffice, if one does not add what has already actually been thought in language.
Editor's note: The title of his work is given more exactly above, p. 18, note.

It can therefore be stated, and it must be stated, for which objects and concepts a language possesses words, what on earth and in heaven, of lifeless and living things, on the animal and human body, what finally of concepts of quality and relation, what of non-sensuous things, it has designated with words.

Where several languages, be it only through the same situation of the nations speaking them, have something in common, as the American languages do, it becomes important to see whether approximately the same circle encompasses the stock of concepts stamped into words in them, and through comparison of many languages one might well, always proceeding from the fact that every language affords a whole of a view of the world, arrive at a certain as it were original circle of this kind, recurring in all.

It would even have to be the same in all, since on the whole the same world presents itself to all nations, if it did not depend on power and opportunity how much of this world is actually transformed into language.

It is easy here to follow the advance of discovery and naming of particular objects, but what is especially important is the seeking out of the modifications of mental concepts, which even in known languages has still by far not been pursued exactly enough.

Within the stock of words of a language there arises the further question: which kinds of objects and concepts have a preponderance in the richness of their expressions? and in this respect too it therefore depends on a separation of them into classes.

For naturally not only the general state of cultivation of nations produces inequalities in this, but also habit, custom and way of life turn a greater manifoldness of expressions now to this, now to that branch of human occupation, and therefore now to this, now to that class of objects and concepts.

General linguistic inquiry must not only proceed from the most general classes, but also lay out its division in such a way that from it there results the manner in which language indicates the concept both before the understanding (98.) and before the ear, which one may call the technique of its designation.

Since for this one must follow its own course, and all need for designation rests in thinking, all words in this respect fall into those concerning the matter, the object, and those concerning the form, the activity of thinking.
For thinking needs words of its own in order to combine, separate and compare concepts and to treat them according to the operations peculiar to it.

These words may in general be called logical or dialectical, and their peculiarity consists in this, that, considered subjectively, they designate what is produced through inner action, but, considered objectively, not objects, nor qualities of objects, but only relations and relationships of concepts and things to one another, and to the understanding through which they are thought.
In the matter of thinking, the domain of the corporeal and the incorporeal naturally forms the principal division.
With respect to the technique of designation, however, there must precede it one more essential in this regard, namely that of words for objects, qualities and actions.

For since objects always stimulate man through salient peculiarity of quality or movement, they also occasion him to designate them chiefly by that, and words for quality and for movement therefore hover, as the highest and most general, in language.
The general words for relationship and relation must also be counted here.

For although these properly, since it is the understanding which relates concepts to one another, fall into the class (117.) of expressions designating its activity, they nevertheless, insofar as one regards them as present on the objects themselves, belong in this respect here as well.
One might wish to object here that this difference is merely a grammatical one.
It is, however, in all languages really lexical and grammatical at once.

For in all of them there are words which originally and according to their concept, thus lexically, even without any grammatical marks, are substantives, adjectives and adverbs, or verbs, and grammar afterwards transforms those belonging in this way to one kind into the two other kinds.

It is so essential to attend to this that in more than one language non-original verbs are formed merely by combination of an original one with a likewise original stem, thus purely lexically, and without any help from grammar.

To these main divisions all the particular ones now attach themselves, which, however, I pass over here, where I am endeavouring to give only the shortest possible outline of the general structure of language.
The same classification of concepts now also facilitates and promotes insight into the technique of designation.

I wish namely here to speak of this not in relation to sounds, but (98.), remaining in the domain of thinking, of the choice of words for things and concepts according to other concepts picked out on them, or referred to them.

These concepts can by far not always be recognized on the words; but to seek out those that can be recognized is uncommonly important, since not only does the individual view of the world given through language first shine forth quite clearly from this, but also in general the whole manner of designation through kinship of concepts, subjective and objective, is one of the most wonderful sides of language.

For the task is no lesser one than to ascend from the first and crudest needs of mutual communication to the totality of the highest ideas and their finest nuances, and always to attach the new word, or the new meaning, to what is already present, since language always stands under the general condition of the possibility of being understood and the speaker may therefore not go beyond what has once been understood further than the hearer is able to follow him.

Language refers incorporeal concepts to corporeal ones, the beings of the corporeal world to the general categories of quality and movement, although this rule is not as universally pervasive as that one.

From both it follows that there is present in language a number of general corporeal concepts of quality and movement which form the main material for designating all the rest, and from which one must therefore chiefly start out in investigating the stock of words of a language.
One can therefore also carry out this investigation from two different sides, from the side of the designating and of the concepts to be designated.

Comparison of this double procedure then shows partly the appropriateness of the designation, partly, in the choice and determination of the designating concepts, the inclination predominant in the people to this or that sensuous mode of intuition, and the kind of mental apprehension, the degree of its clarity, determinateness, purity and depth.
It is therefore by no means necessary that a language should possess a number of root-words which one could regard as the origin of all the rest.
Even where such are present, derived words too, and most frequently, are used for designating new concepts.
But consideration of root-words cannot be bypassed here.
They have namely evidently a double validity, a grammatical and a lexical one.
They cannot appear in connected speech at all, or only under certain conditions, without grammatical change, and they serve as stem-words for derivation and composition.
There are languages in which it has become lexicographic custom, as in Sanskrit and Welsh, to trace every word back to one of the assumed roots.
But there is probably none of this structure in which the groundlessness of such a procedure could not be shown by striking examples.
Beside the majority of words willingly and easily derivable from the roots, there are always still many which can be brought under them only by forced and playful artifice.
Language knows, however, yet another means of increasing its richness in words besides the formation of individual expressions.

It designates namely, on whole series of words, determinations common to them all, creates expressions not through new word-sounds, but through alteration of existing ones determined according to rules.
This often happens through mere composition, but also through derivation, and indeed both through agglutination and through inflexion.

Of this kind are the *Patronymica*, *Gentilitia*, *Abstracta*, the property words (a kind running through almost all American languages), the causal-volitive verbs, etc. Since one has once accustomed oneself, for reasons in practical respects much to be approved,

to take into grammar everything that can be brought under rules, and to leave to the dictionary only the alphabetical listing of the individual item, one now usually finds these methods of designation in grammars, but they evidently belong to the formation of the stock of words, not to the combination of speech.
Their more exact and deeper investigation is, however, important, because one can judge from it how logically exact and philosophically correct language proceeds therein.

For since kinds formed according to rules are in question here, it depends on how the ground of division is apprehended, whether all species flowing from it are exhausted, indeed even whether in the choice of designating these concepts through derivation, thus according to laws that must be learnt, or through composition, thus in an immediately intelligible way, chance or a rule has prevailed.

For it would be more in accordance with logical purposefulness to undertake formation according to laws only where the kinds to be designated can be derived purely from concepts, in number and quality, not where, as with the concept of property, an individual factual relation determines the kind of word.

There is also another case by which the logical appropriateness and completeness of linguistic designation must be tested, namely by the concepts which together fill up a sphere, and where the question now is whether language possesses for each of them an expression of its own, and whether the reciprocal relation of these concepts is designated on the expressions themselves.
As examples I need cite here only the dimensions of space and the points of the compass.

Several languages in the former combine under the same expression two different ones, such as *schmal* 'narrow, slender' and *eng* 'narrow, tight', *breit* 'broad' and *gross* 'large'; in the latter, in many languages, as in German and Sanskrit (in the former in relation to the course of the sun dividing the day, in the latter in relation to an assumed standpoint according to which one determines the sides), the expression preserves the uniformity of the concepts; in others, as in Latin, this is disturbed, or there is none at all.

The whole investigation of the stock of words of languages, here only indicated in the outermost outline, aims at recognising as exactly and completely as possible the system of its formation, so that one may survey how much, what among given possibilities, and in what manner it designates?

For that reason the domain of what is to be designated according to its different divisions (113—118.), the stock of concepts which for the purpose of designation one refers to others (119—122.), and finally the extent of word-sounds, both of root-words and of derived and compound words, according to the character and treatment of the sounds (73—82.), must be gone through.

When this has been done, one possesses a concept of the material which language offers to speech, and now has only still (105.) to consider the feeling accompanying the words, their reaction upon the soul.
This was hitherto spoken of only as a part of the content of the word; here, however, the peculiarity of language in the treatment of all words is now to be gathered together.
As in what is to be designated the world appears, so here man appears, and both related to one another as both present themselves in the same language.

The easier or more sluggish excitability of feeling, the brighter or darker colour of the imagination, the more prosaic or poetic direction become manifest here as causes, as one recognised them in the objective formation of words as results.
It would therefore also be useless to go into further detail here.

It suffices to remark that what is at issue here is to consider subjectively the stock of words hitherto tested objectively, in order to see whether a certain uniformity of the feeling that predominated in word-formation can be discovered, and what kind of national peculiarity is revealed in it?
For this feeling acting upon formation is the same which afterwards always also accompanies the word in use.

I call it feeling, partly in order to gather together in the most general word everything in which language can bear upon itself the traces of the human way of being, partly, however, and especially, because that of which we are speaking here really acts at the moment of its activity only as feeling, not in clear and distinct consciousness.

For otherwise there lies quite especially in it also the purely intellectual direction, as well as the whole subjective effect which the words of a language, because they belong to it, produce differently from those of another.
That this in turn also contributes to the objective representation of the world through language is self-evident.
But many separations and divisions necessary in the science of language lead not so much to really different objects, as merely to consideration of different sides of the same object.

If, e.g., there lies in the word-formation of a language the direction of keeping the mind predominantly in the sphere of easy combination of ideas for the purposes of life, it will be this intellectual mood especially which also usually accompanies the incorporeal expressions of the language.
But at the same time it will arise from this that these expressions, in their designation too, themselves take their objects more from the superficial side.
Nevertheless, in order to know language completely from this side, the double juxtaposition of this objective character and of this subjective influence upon it will always remain necessary.
For the latter will afterwards also appear uniformly in other parts of the structure of language, namely e.g. in the joining together of speech.

The subjective mood which cooperates in word-formation and is produced again by the formed word, since cause and effect always step into each other's place, is attached by far less firmly to the dead word than is the designation of the object.
If, therefore, even the latter, as we have seen (84.), is exposed to changes in the course of time, this is far more the case with the subjective impression.

Elevated words sink down to common ones, poetic words become prosaic, and vice versa, the whole direction of a nation's thinking and feeling alters imperceptibly, and as this in turn (125.) reacts upon designation, sound and meaning indeed remain apparently and on the whole the same, but the altered apprehension of the latter nevertheless shows closer examination something different in it.

Thus especially to incorporeal expressions: *Seele* 'soul', *Geist* 'spirit, mind', *Herz* 'heart', *Gemüth* 'inner disposition, mind', etc., a very different sense gradually insinuates itself through mere apprehension.

Conversely, however, as happens, perhaps through the influence of individual writers, in some principal expressions, the mental direction of the nation gradually alters, and this alteration then reacts upon the whole language in increased proportion.
Of these changes in the feeling accompanying words, whether they exert influence on their meanings or not, isolated words seldom bear any recognisable traces on themselves.
Only where literary monuments are extant can they be traced.

Since the causes of these changes also lie solely in the nation's mode of apprehension, but very sudden and abrupt transitions are possible in the interior of man, languages undergo these transformations, precisely the most decisive for their innermost being, more quickly, frequently and strongly than those through deflection of meanings too as a whole, and through reshaping of sounds.

Their study belongs chiefly to the history of mental formation; the study of language often leaves them wholly outside its circle, and does not do wrong in this if it wishes to restrict itself merely to the material, in a certain measure cruder, part of language, but must necessarily include it within itself if language, as is the purpose here, is to be represented in its complete relation to man.
