sentences.english: β. Vocabulary.
A word is a sound that designates a concept.
In the word, therefore, there is always unity of sound, which where sounds are combined is brought about by the accent, and unity of concept.
The simple word is the true individual in language.

For it contains completely the whole act of the understanding that belongs to language; indeed it is itself the form in which the mind sets the object that it has transformed into its subjectivity outside itself again, as object (39.); but what results when the word itself is analysed in turn, the syllable and the letter, is no longer language, but only an element of it.
All words, the compound ones included, are the constituents, the material of discourse, and the vocabulary of a language therefore contains the whole thought-material of a nation.

The word shares the whole nature of language as developed in the foregoing: it has the same objectivity and subjectivity (40.), exerts the same power over human beings (42.), and is equally subject to their freedom (51.); it forms objects into the ideal world of its own which in language generally takes the place of the real one (39.).

The peculiar apprehension of things by language lies chiefly in this, that the individual subjectivity, always remaining the same, takes and treats all the constituents of the language in the same way and attaches itself to each of them; and this apprehension derives more from the ideal than from the material part of languages, more from the mode of presentation that a language gives than from the sounds used in it.

The words which, in little-altered tones and designating definite objects, pass from generation to generation and from nation to nation can therefore bear this peculiarity only in a scarcely visible way; it reveals itself only in their use, and in the way in which they mutually complete, limit and determine one another.

Where, therefore, as with the languages of uncultivated nations, this use is known only from meagre specimens of the language, the mere knowledge of words, which is for that very reason also incomplete, does not suffice to fathom the peculiarity of the language precisely on its most important side.
First printing of this chapter: Internationale Zeitschrift für allgemeine Sprachwissenschaft 1, 385–411 (1884).
The number of words possible in a language depends on the number of syllables possible in it (62.a.) and on the particular rules and habits that prevail in it for word-formation (62.b.).
This number can properly be determined only where it is comparatively small and is actually exhausted, wholly or for the most part, by the language.
This can be the case almost only in the languages with monosyllabic words.

It is striking that the Chinese language, its poverty in spoken words notwithstanding, nevertheless does not carry every one of the possible words through all the existing kinds of intonation. Still less does it combine all final vowels with every initial consonant.
If, however, these languages are grouped together as a genus of their own, one must understand well in what manner this is done.
This division cannot be called purely factual.

For a large part of all languages, however many-syllabled, can be traced back by analysis to monosyllabic roots, and if one goes back in thought to the origin of languages, the most natural thing is to devote to the simple concept only a simple sound as well.
Yet this must not be understood as though every stem-word necessarily had to be monosyllabic.

For in our investigation of language, in which we are never able to go back to the beginning, the concept of the stem-word is itself only a relational concept, and each of our languages may have begun with many polysyllabic words alongside monosyllabic ones.

On the other hand, the monosyllabic languages too do not possess this property in its purity, and when in them two words come together to form a compound concept, everything depends solely on the accent, which either joins them or, still thrusting each out singly, separates them.

Now to decide whether this separation also holds the concepts further apart in the understanding, or whether the connection of the concepts allows the peculiarity of the pronunciation to be regarded only as such, not as a division of words, may well border on impossibility.

On the other hand, it may well be maintained with good reason that the splitting of the tones, where the close connection makes the concepts into one, disturbs the influence which the division of discourse into correct and appropriate word-wholes produces upon the mind.
In each individual case it may be indifferent whether the division of sound keeps pace with the division of thought or not.
But in the mass the importance is unmistakable, and the thoroughgoing cutting up of the sounds into single syllables must act unfavourably on the flow of thoughts.

However, in China itself inquiry has probably never been directed to these subtler mental influences of language, and in nature a disproportion usually rights itself again and again through other circumstances arising alongside it, so that on the whole the same phenomenon emerges once more as where the disproportion is not present.
Even the concept of monosyllabic languages must therefore be understood with a certain restriction, and the polysyllabic ones may originally have been monosyllabic.

The division of words that underlies this classification rests, even in respect of the sounds, on circumstances which, as has just been shown, are all the more difficult to judge as they presuppose no exact knowledge of the living delivery of discourse.
Nevertheless, the monosyllabic structure of a small number of languages remains a most remarkable phenomenon which, precisely because of its rarity, deserves the most attentive consideration.
It is an entirely false manner of presentation to regard these languages, like children's languages as it were, as having remained standing at a stage of original imperfection.
The causes of monosyllabism must certainly be sought quite differently and much deeper.
Since, however, this property is foreign to the American languages, I have wished only to assign it here its fitting place in the edifice of language in general.
The same holds, in the polysyllabic languages, of the uniformity in the structure of the stem-words which is met with, for example, in the Semitic languages.

Where word-formation is bound to no such fixed form, the number of possible words remains indeterminate, and a multitude of concurring circumstances, of which an account can only seldom be given, determines which of them are actually called into existence.
But one must always assume that each has arisen through another that existed before it.
For all changes in language take place (43.) gradually, and it is always only what has already been heard, wholly or in part, that is repeated.
The investigation of word-sounds therefore finds itself everywhere at the middle of a chain whose beginning remains inaccessible to it.

It hardly needs the cautionary remark, however, that not all languages still extant need on that account be parts of the same chain, since (46.) there could be different developments of words which did not come into connection with one another for a long time, or never did.

Since, however, the sameness of the organs of speech and of their laws everywhere makes possible the same word-sounds, and only a certain number of them, the mere identity or kinship of tone cannot by itself (47.) decide the question of its historical or physiological difference.

Kinship can be conceived in two ways: through derivation, in that the simpler tone becomes something more or less compound by suffixing, prefixing or insertion; and through assonance, in that the simple tone sounds again, likewise simple but altered, or a kindred idea is designated by a kindred tone.

From this origin of every word out of another word, at most those imitated from natural sounds might have to be excepted, which do indeed usually likewise pass from generation to generation and from nation to nation, but can also arise suddenly, although even in this case they will always conform to the sound-analogy of the rest of the language.

Here, where only the course of word-formation in a given language is to be investigated, the sole concern is to analyse the compound word-sounds into ever simpler ones, so far as this is possible, to develop the analogy of this composition, and to compare the simplest words thus found with one another in turn in their sound-relations.
From this there result, on the one hand, the laws and habits of the nations' word-formation, and on the other the extent, the completeness and the antique character of their word-structure.

To the former belong the alterations of words through the series of vowels, the insertions and alterations of consonants, the expansions of words by fore- and after-sounds, the syllable repetitions and transpositions.
In all this the cruder or finer sense of language of the nations can very often be recognized.
The more closely a language is taken from one already fully formed, the less it ascends to simple sounds, which in the vocabulary of several of these are scarcely met with at all.

Only where considerable tribes have for centuries, in great freedom from foreign admixture, carried their language onward from generation to generation, and the origin is lost in obscurity, does there appear that wide and antique structure in which long lineages of words can be traced back to their fundamental sounds, in which these still have meaning in their simplicity, every analogy proves itself in numerous examples, every sound-quality that stands with others in the same sphere or genus finds several of these or all of them beside it, and in which, accordingly, strict analogy leads the mind through a far-embracing system of word-sonorities.

Now this, apart from the influence of such fullness and regularity upon use, also reacts in itself upon the nation, in clear consciousness as in obscure feeling, and the generation of language within it becomes more fruitful for everything with which it stands in contact when the world of ideas is joined by a world of tones that orders itself easily and wonderfully.

The structure of such a language links every individual to far more distant times, to a far more original condition of the human race, to a seemingly infinite mass of thoughts and sensations that once existed and that nevertheless always in some way touch one another and call one another forth again.
Herein lies (55.) the system of rules of word-formation, which, even in the merely lexical comparison of languages, one has to distinguish from the tones themselves.
Its foundation is the sound-system.

For the finer and more intellectual the ear and the sense of language prove to be in this, the more carefully is every modification of tone that arises, perhaps at first only by chance, through the insertion of an aspiration, a vowel or a nasal sound, heeded and carried through the similar cases, and the more analogically are other alterations of like kind modelled upon it.

From kindred nations the fundamental features of this system pass over into kindred languages, and the likeness in kind of languages can in many respects be recognized more correctly by lexical analogy than by grammatical analogy.
For the former does not rest, like the latter, on general laws of thought, but attaches itself directly to the tone.
But the more individual a likeness in kind is, the more surely it points to a historical connection.

Yet careful note must be taken of the cases in which words in whose structure analogies of this kind are indicated have passed over into other languages without these analogies themselves, i.e. without the feeling for them in the other nation, and therefore without further development by that nation, and now become parts of a language in which no such structure exists at all in such perfection, or in which a different system of it exists.

From this inner connection of words, in their sounds as well, it now follows of itself that the words of several languages may not, for the purpose of discovering their likeness in kind, be compared directly with one another, but that a comparison of them within each language singly must first precede.
The alphabetical juxtaposition of the words of different languages tears each of these languages out of its natural connection.

But once the comparison of the words of one language among themselves has been carried out, two objects present themselves for the comparison with another: the rules of lexical analogy and the fundamental sounds, and, together with the former, the compound words actually formed according to these rules that have passed from one language into the other.
A comparison that carries its warrant within itself can take place only in this way.

If, however, as is very often the case, from want of aids, or because a language has no inner structure so perspicuously carried out, and because even the structure that exists is never quite completely recognized, one is thrown back upon the direct comparison of words, one must nevertheless first investigate the two words to be compared as exactly as possible, each in its own language, with respect to their origin, so as not to regard words that are really different as alike in kind on account of a merely apparent similarity of sound.

Thus one might take the Coptic *hrosch* and the Sanskrit *rôsha*, both of which mean 'anger', to be alike in kind, since the *h* here could just as well be a mere aspiration of the *r* as it is in *hloili*, which is also *loili*. But more careful comparison shows that *hrosch* has arisen from *horsch*, which has the same meaning, as *hroyr* has from *hoyrooy* and *heri*, and that this similarity of sound with the Indian word is therefore merely accidental.

In all the respects considered here, regard has been had only to the dependence of word-formation on the nation's treatment of tone, to the way in which the nation gives extent and variety to the stock of its word-sounds.

But word-formation is also, and chiefly, accompanied by regard for meaning, and if, for example, the origin of *λαμβάνω* from *λάβω* is mere alteration of tone, that of *legen* ['to lay'] from *liegen* ['to lie'] brings with it a nuance of sense.

Word-formation by composition rests entirely on meaning; in it several concepts are always combined, either into a new third concept or, as in formation by prefixes and suffixes, merely for the varied determination of the principal concept.
The sound-relations play a part in this only occasionally and in a subordinate way.

In the choice of sounds for concepts, language naturally lets itself be guided by the clearer and more obscure relations which feeling and imagination, in accordance with the individuality of the nations, find among them.

Historically, however, this is lost in the times of the invention of language, which no investigation can any longer reach, and through the gradual transformation of language, in which now the tone is deflected little by little further from the fundamental tone, now the concept from the fundamental concept, this relation between tone and meaning very often undergoes a complete change.

Moreover, the feeling on which it rests, by its nature a less determinate one, differs in different peoples, and precisely those nations that possess more original languages, i.e. languages bearing fewer traces of great upheavals, tolerate fewer colliding consonants in their syllables, and thus lack one more means of determining the character of the word-sound.

It is therefore by no means an unusual phenomenon to see strong and even repugnant concepts paired with gentle and soft sounds, and vice versa, and in historical investigations of language no weight whatever is to be laid on this analogy.

Fantasy and ingenuity find in it a wide but highly insecure ground, and for every ten examples that demonstrate such agreement of tone with meaning one comes upon a far greater number in which it is lacking.
On the other hand, it would be equally incorrect to turn attention away from it entirely.
For it cannot be denied that in languages of great age and of wide and varied word-structure the feeling of such an unmistakable agreement forces itself upon one more frequently than in others.

But where, in a mother tongue that has remained unmixed, this agreement continues for centuries to act upon the same nation, it heightens and strengthens the influence of language, in which everything depends on making of the word, through the closest fusion of tone with concept, an entity of its own that hovers between the human being and the world, at once dependent on and independent of both.
This is especially visible in German and the languages dependent on it.

The word-sounds do indeed pass, together with their meanings, from generation to generation and from tribe to tribe; but since the concept is more mobile than the sound perceptible to the senses, and, according to relations that lie now in the concept itself, now in the individual, now also in external circumstances, forms easier transitions, deflections of the meanings arise more frequently than deflections of the tone.

The word-sounds may therefore be regarded as forms which have been preserved down to us from hoary antiquity and have stored up within themselves a more or less changing import, through which, however, there always winds a thread, even if often one that connects only loosely.
Already to this extent a separation of the word as sound and as concept, one admittedly not present in nature, becomes necessary in the investigation of the structure of language.

For the continuous series of presentations requires, just as the continuous series of tones does, division into units of thought corresponding to the word-sounds, by means of which ideal Objects can be apprehended and connected.

To each such unit of thought, and hence to each word, there corresponds an object, either one that can be pointed out corporeally in nature, or one formed by the mind more or less independently of sense perception.

For although in this latter case the word itself is this object, one must nevertheless distinguish the word in general and in itself from the word as thought at a determinate moment by a determinate individual, just as one must, in the same way, with language as a whole.
The word causes the soul to present to itself the object given in it.

This presentation must be distinguished from the object; it can be individually different, and must be so, since it is determined on all sides, whereas the object, as Object, can only ever be grasped more generally; besides the objective part, which relates to the object, it has a subjective part lying in the manner of apprehension, both in the intellectual view and in the sentiment accompanying this.

Again, however, it scarcely needs remarking that this separation rests only on abstraction; that the word can have no abode outside thinking, and just as little can its object, if this is an incorporeal one; that the word itself is each time wholly produced by the mind; that it truly has its completeness and individuality only in the thinking of each occasion; and that, as a constituent of language, as Object of linguistic investigation, it is only a general form which can be individualized in different ways, though ways limited by its nature.
Even with objects of sense this remains the case, since they themselves never become directly present to the soul, but always only that presentation of them which the word gives of them.

On the fact that every word of a language possesses a certain breadth for the possibility of diverse presentations rests the possibility that the modes of presentation of quite different individualities of persons and of ages unite in the same language, and that, for all the sameness of the general language, each (50.) can nevertheless have its own.

For understanding is not a meeting of the modes of presentation in an indivisible point, but a meeting of spheres of thought, of which the more general part coincides, while the more individual part projects beyond.

By this the mental progress of the human race becomes possible, in that every enlargement of thinking that has been won can pass into the possession of others without laying fetters in them upon the freedom which is necessary for appropriation and for new enlargement, and in that at the same time the forms of thinking, the languages, undergo the changes which are prescribed to them, as to everything that is bound to earthly appearance, in the course of their development.

In every meaning of a word, therefore, attention is to be directed to how it leaves the individual mode of presentation free and how it determines it, and a history of words and of their individual meanings can be carried through all the different ways in which they have been taken and used.

The concept raised to the clarity and determinacy of the word is always the result of the cooperation of the whole power of the soul, and since it is the peculiarity of the word to call forth this concept by the tone, as if by an electric shock, its effect radiates through the whole soul in all directions.

The unity of a power cannot be split into parts; nevertheless, in the formation and the influence of the word three great and principal relations stand out, under which each word can be considered and examined: its logical construction, its sensuous validity and its impression on feeling.

Each of these three items, however, appears in the word again in a twofold manner, since one must distinguish the presentation of the object itself (85.) from that which the word, by its formation and origin, gives of it, and of these two presentations neither cancels the other, but both enter into a certain relation to one another.
The word gives the concept shape, and, through the tone, immediately before the ear and mediately before all the sensuous powers of the soul, sensuous validity.

The word apprehends every concept as a general one and, strictly taken, always designates classes of reality, even when it is a proper name, since it then gathers together all the states of what is designated that differ in time and space (presenting it as a class in which it is contained in all these states just as different individuals are contained in a generic concept).
But it makes itself, and hence also the concept contained in it, into an individual of the language.

It can therefore take the concept only from a single standpoint, yet may give up nothing of its import, and this is achieved in that the word imparts to the soul, in the direction of those three principal relations, a determinate stimulus, through which the generation of the concept takes place completely indeed, but from one sharply determined side.

Thereby there arise, in the words of like meaning in several languages, different presentations of the same object, and this constitution of the word chiefly contributes to each language's affording a world-view of its own.
Just as language, and in it the word, generalizes the individual nature of the world, so it spiritualizes that nature which, in outer and inner perception, is material in kind.
But just as the word itself in turn becomes an individual in language, so too it becomes corporeal in language by taking on tone, and serves the mind as material for new activity.

The one and the other, however, take place at once and in indivisible unity, synthetically, and generality and individuality, spirituality and materiality permeate one another in the word; which, since those concepts would otherwise cancel one another, is possible only because the word, thought as a constituent of language outside the soul, is nothing but a stimulus to thinking, whereas, thought as a completed concept in the soul, it is thinking itself, and because this unceasing developing of the general and non-sensuous out of the individual and sensuous, and its returning into the same, belongs peculiarly to the human mental power.

If we now look back at the three principal directions mentioned above (87.) in which the word stimulates the soul, the word can possess sensuous validity and validity for sentiment only in so far as it is able to maintain these for itself in the domain of intellectuality.

This, however, happens only in that this import of sense and feeling is at once, and again synthetically, annihilated as material and preserved as form, which is the work of the imagination, the mediator between the opposed natures in humanity.

Since the word's import for the understanding, too, can unite with the sensuous only in the imagination's domain, this domain is properly the sphere in which the word hovers, in that the imagination gathers together the collective powers of the soul for the producing or the understanding of the word.

The manner in which the word, always in those three directions, brings the objects of outer and inner perception before the soul may be called what is objective in it, its matter; the manner, however, in which the faculties of the soul enter, in those directions, into relation with one another and fuse into the unity of cooperation may be called what is subjective in it, its form.

Both lie undeniably in language and in each single one of its words; having been the individuality of the speakers, it has fastened itself to the sounds, and through them returns into living individuality.

For the wonderful kind of embodiment of a mental begetting, which brings forth a like begetting in another, is after all the truly peculiar nature of language, and rests chiefly on its principal constituent, the word.
Form, however, is still more important than matter.

For it attaches to the whole language, and so even when the language, as a dead or foreign one, is apprehended by a very different individuality, it nevertheless compels that individuality to adopt its mode of intuition, by entwining it on all sides with that mode.

Matter not only cannot do this; the particular mode of presentation of the object does not even always remain recognizable in the word, or at least is no longer felt as it was at the word's origin; the individuality of the word is lost in the generality of the concept.
I have already pointed to this above (87.), in the distinction between the presentation of the object and the word's presentation of it.

This distinction does indeed become possible only because the word, as embodied concept, is gradually adapted by very different individualities to different modes of intuition, in which the use made of it on each occasion does not portray the object at all as the first inventor did; but, so understood, whole series of examples of it can be pointed out.

The expressions for corporeal objects have certainly for the most part arisen from properties that were especially striking in them, and are nothing other than substantives that have become adjectives; non-sensuous concepts are designated metaphorically after corporeal ones; grammatical concepts, which merely determine the connection of discourse, after words for concepts of things.
In all these cases the character of the original designation very often, indeed for the most part, perishes, and the concept of the object, taken generally or in some other way, steps into its place.

With the Indian *dwîpa* for elephant, the property of drinking twice, through the trunk and the mouth, has hardly always been thought of; and it occurs to few who use the German *Vernunft* ['reason'] and *zurück* ['back'] that the former comes from *vernehmen* ['to perceive, to hear'] and the latter from *Rücken* ['the back'].
Many words which formerly had no such accessory meaning at all are later used only jocularly, ironically or contemptuously.

Thus the matter of the word changes; even between the same tone and the same object designated by it the mind finds room for play of comfortable breadth in which to insert differently nuanced kinds of presentation; properly speaking, however, under the same audible sound a different word is uttered each time.

For only what is actually thought or spoken is the word proper; what is handed down by inheritance in the language, dead as it were, is only the envelope, animated ever anew and always somewhat differently.
In what is thought or spoken, matter and form are always determined at once by the character of the word and of the language and by that of the speaker.
This coincides with what was remarked above (86.), that the nature of the word, even within the same language, permits each individual to have, up to a certain degree, a language of their own.
It differs, however, in that the former occurs even where the matter and form of the word-sound are perfectly felt, whereas here the opposite case is being spoken of.
Thus a twofold breadth of the sound-form, as envelope of the concept, reveals itself here.
When in the words of a language the original mode of intuition of objects is gradually effaced, it cannot be denied that a certain individuality and sensuous liveliness perishes in it.
But it cannot on that account be said that the language does not perhaps gain thereby on the other side.
For the excellences of languages are not determined by the partial wealth of images and concepts which they bring to the soul, but by their effect on thinking and sentiment in general.

Thus, for example, the designation of objects by their properties cited above (90.), so long as it is alive in a language, affords a greater fullness of intuition; but it also has, not to mention other, lesser ones, the disadvantage that it restricts too one-sidedly the freedom in presenting the object to oneself, and that, forming substantives too visibly out of adjectives, it disturbs the agreement in which language, following nature in its own form too, must use, for the expression of beings that are self-subsistent in nature, words likewise endowed with self-subsistence.

Far more fitting in its effect is the accord of the concept with the sound according to an obscure feeling of affinity (83.), since the soul is thereby attuned and guided, but not restricted in the manner of presentation.

When linguistic investigation turns to these relations, seeks them out in words without reading them into them, and in this way awakens the nation's linguistic sense, which is always akin, even unconsciously, to the mother tongue, and thereby brings about clearer insight and a finer feeling for the language, the original individuality of words can again come more brightly to light, and now subordinates itself, without doing further harm, to the apprehension of objects that has through time become freer and more intellectual.
Not easily will two languages maintain, in the form of their words, a perfect equilibrium between the different stimuli which the soul thereby receives.

One of these stimuli will predominate over the other, and the force too will differ with which these stimuli strike together in the concept into the presentation of the object, on which the clarity and determinacy of thinking chiefly rests.
Researches of this kind can be made only on highly cultivated languages, yet mere feeling too perceives the differences.
In one a greater sensuous clarity prevails, another attunes feeling more, a third contents itself more drily with logical determination.
The changing orientation of the nation can modify this character, but, being unceasingly subject to its influences, can never abandon it.
It also in part determines the use that is made of the language, the more poetic, philosophical or scientific character of its literature, and is in turn determined by this.

With the matter of words the nature of the objects now comes in as well, and with every word there accordingly arise the questions: what does the word gather together as its object? how does it designate what is thus gathered together? and what accessory concept does it, in accordance with accompanying feeling, connect with this designation?

If these questions are put one after another from a twofold standpoint, first from that of one language with regard to the manifoldness of objects, then from the standpoint of the objects with regard to the words of several languages, the relation of the designation to what is designated is exhausted, at least as regards direction.
For language proceeds in word-formation in a uniform manner, and it is this manner that must be explored by examining a considerable number of words.
The material import of words seems to be determined of itself by the objects of thinking.

The comparative investigation of several languages, however, shows the contrary, and since the word depends not immediately on the object but on the apprehension of it, and indeed many objects are first formed by the soul, it must necessarily be so.

The first law prevailing here is that of a correct division of the thought-material by language, or, otherwise expressed, that the object of the word be circumscribed by firm boundaries, contain everything that belongs to the completion of its concept, and nothing that is not essential to it but only accidentally attaches to it.

Even with expressions for corporeal objects, their meanings are not always conformed to the firm boundaries of nature but waver about between them; still more frequently this indeterminacy is found in intellectual designations; and it is quite usual, in the languages with which we are here primarily concerned, to find admixed with the concept determinations which disturb its generality and which it must carry about with it only to the detriment of distinctness.
On the other hand, however, there are also in several languages new and excellently formed concepts which must count as true enlargements of thinking.

For the possession of a word for a concept not hitherto thought within these boundaries is, when it concerns a mass of thought-material that can enter into thinking in a way that furthers the gaining of enlarged views, of immeasurable gain.

In this distribution of concepts among words there is revealed, in the first instance, the nation's sense for correct and sharp apprehension of nature and for logical exactness; but in higher respects there issues from it the mind's happy power of creation.

Certainly, however, one may only very seldom imagine this as though a new word were given to a purely thought concept; usually only a word hitherto taken in a lower or less determinate meaning is restamped.
Of this kind in Sanskrit are *kaṭi*, *taṭa*, *śrôṇi*, *nitamba*, all of which indicate the region of the body about the hips with indeterminate delimitation.
Here one may cite the Sanskrit *nyâya* and *yôga*.
The second law in respect of the content of words is that the word should not comprise within itself too many meanings, connected with one another by too loose bonds of affinity.
This is found in some languages more than in others; complaint is made of it in Chinese and Sanskrit in particular.

Yet it should not be forgotten that this complaint for the most part touches only the deficiency of the dictionaries, which, without order or reflection, let all the meanings in which the word is found in individual passages follow one upon another, and pick out from each passage precisely the most determinate meaning, into which the connection of the concepts forces the natural and simple sense of the word.

Were this duly appreciated, and were the periods and genres of usage distinguished, that multiplicity of meanings, which at present is admittedly troublesome, especially to the beginner, would melt away considerably.

Where it cannot be denied, however, it coincides on the one hand with the indeterminacy censured above (96.), which admits more than one determination of the concept and hence several concepts; but on the other hand it can also arise from too acute a spinning-out of a concept into all the threads proceeding from it, or from a fondness for all too bold metaphors, and hence be peculiar precisely to the languages of very ingenious nations.
With the multiplicity of meanings of words, however, one must not confuse the comprehensive extent of their meaning.

With the latter the meaning nevertheless remains simple, and a language that truly furthers reflection must have fixed the thought precisely at the highest levels of abstraction too, or at the lowest of individualizing determination (since such words can arise at both).

Only the plurality of concrete meanings standing side by side, and the arbitrary application of general ones to one of the many comprehended under them, disturbs the determinacy of expression and ease of intelligibility.

By the manner of designation of the concept in the word I do not here understand designation by the tone, although the kind of which we are speaking here determines the tone and sometimes coincides with it.
Otherwise, however, the tone in general (73–82.), and in particular in relation to meaning (83.), has already been spoken of above.
Here it is the content of the word, that is, the concept, that is in question.

But the concept can be given neither in its definition nor, if it belongs to a corporeal object, in the whole essence of that object; the word must shape it into unity (88.); that, therefore, by which the word indicates it to the mind of the hearer is, even as concept, its designation.

Originally this designation (which properly is such only in relation to the hearer, but on the side of the speaker is an apprehension) lies in every word: in those modelled on natural sounds, in the sounding of the objects; in others for corporeal things, in other properties of theirs; in intellectual ones, in the metaphors chosen to indicate them.

For when the concept was clothed in a tone, the tongue had after all to let itself be determined by something in the choice of it, and this could only be this mode of intuition, which gathers the whole concept together in one point.

This mode of intuition itself, however, can only be thought of as sensuous, partly because it is to guide the choice of the tone, partly because the whole of word-formation (89.) hovers in the sphere of the imagination.

In most cases, however, this sensuous mode of apprehension of the object, which preceded the tone, or arose together with it yet always determining it, can no longer be traced, and then it still adheres merely in the effect exerted on the tone, and sometimes no longer even in this in any recognizable way.

In the former case the sound-character of the word (its hardness or softness, its brightness or dullness, etc.), in the latter merely the audible sound of the articulated tones themselves, is the designation of the word's content.
Examples are furnished by the three German words *Fliege* ['fly'], *Krähe* ['crow'], *Gans* ['goose'].

In the first, the designation of the concept is the incessantly recurring flying by which the creature becomes so especially troublesome; in the second, the cry of the bird; in the third, the mere word, which derives from the Indian and cannot be explained there either.
Similar examples are afforded by the words for mental concepts, with and without recognizable metaphors.
This kind of designation of the concept could be called the self-meaning of words.
For by it they really do differ from other words devoted to the same object.

It is in many respects important to inquire whether in a language such a self-meaning belongs to many words, and also to distinguish the case already indicated (91.): whether it is still generally felt by the people, or only still lies there recognizable to the investigator.

Since the predominance of self-meanings must probably rightly be regarded as the more original state in languages, inferences can be drawn from it as to the changes that have taken place in a language.

The self-meanings themselves, however, so far as they reveal themselves with reliability, are important to investigate, because they show the direction in which a people has apprehended nature and has appropriated what is mental to language in sensuous envelopment.

Since, however, one is supposed here to be on historical ground, one must take good care not to concede too much to acumen and imagination in this, and must confine oneself to that alone to which sure traces of formation lead.

The sensuous material of the word, of which we are speaking here, is the handle by which the mind apprehends the intellectual concepts, and if one wishes to remain faithful to the course of nature, one must think of their designation in language not as descending from the concept to the designation, but, conversely, as ascending to the concept.

It is everywhere so in humanity that out of appearances which come into existence, as if by chance, through the mere fertility of generative powers, a whole builds itself up, from which the unity of an idea afterwards shines forth to the observing mind; and it is no different in language.

In the motley manifoldness of tones which the perception of nature, the need for communication and social loquacity elicit, the soul discovers the mental relations, and does so the more frequently and with the more genius, the more it is itself possessed of higher intellectual power and a finer linguistic sense, and coins the existing words in meanings corresponding to those relations.

Not through a brooding over the material of ideas that is, as it were, dull and occupied with dividing and dissecting, but through the fecundation of the natural mass of tones by an active mind always directed towards what is higher, there arises in languages a rich and deep import of ideas in words ingeniously appropriated to it.
The word, as designation of the concept, is akin to the sign and the symbol.
This, however, is the place to fix these three concepts exactly, and to show that the word does indeed share properties with the other two, but is, in its innermost nature, different from both.

In so far as it calls forth the concept by its sound, it does indeed fulfil the purpose of a sign; but it passes entirely out of the class of signs in that what is designated has an existence independent of its sign, whereas the concept itself first receives its completion through the word, and the two cannot be separated from one another.
To misjudge this, and to regard words as mere signs, is the fundamental error that destroys all linguistic science and all correct appreciation of language.
In so far as the word transforms the concept into a sensuous material before the imagination, it resembles the symbol.

For it slips a shape beneath the idea, and, in the case of a corporeal object, abstracts from the totality of its reality, in that it holds the object fast by one characteristic mark and designates it in this mark by something foreign to it, a tone.
The sound thus, in this way like a hieroglyph, encloses the concept within itself.

In the symbol the sensuous and the non-sensuous, mutually permeating one another, are regarded as one, the latter revealing itself in the former, the former expanding into the latter; idea and corporeal material coincide.

With the word, too, the concept cannot be cleanly separated from the sound: not in itself, since it cannot be thought without language; not from the sound that is determinately its own in a language, because it at the same time bears that sound's individuality in itself.
Nevertheless the word is altogether different from the symbol.

The symbol requires a complete, self-subsistent natural form, which can also be considered without any relation to an indwelling idea, but out of which, as soon as it proves itself to be a symbol, the idea shines forth from all its parts.

The sound in the word (as its sensuous material, corresponding to that natural form) is, by contrast, nothing without relation to the concept, since its exclusive vocation is to call the concept forth in shaped form.

There is therefore a quite different coincidence of the sensuous and the non-sensuous in the symbol and in the word; in the latter, sound and concept, without admitting even a separation, and each incomplete by itself, are one and make up one being, but the sound in a certain measure yields to the concept, which it is only to call forth and shape.

In the symbol the natural form is self-subsistent together with the idea permeating it, and pre-eminently asserts its rights; the two are the same, since from every point of the one the other shines forth, but they are not one.
The natural form remains, even without an idea thought in it, in everything by which it had validity in the symbol, like the body when the soul leaves it.

Words and word-sounds can, however, like all other objects, be treated as symbols in their constitution and number and in connection with their meaning, and it is probably thus to be understood when it is told of the Egyptian priests that they celebrated the gods by sounding out the seven vowels one after another.

The symbolizing understanding and the sense and the genius for language therefore stand in natural opposition to one another.
They also accustom the mind to a quite different measure of lingering in the succession of presentations, which is one of the chief points in the formation of intellects in individuals and nations.

Symbolizing leads to immersion in the individual object, whose shell must, as it were, be penetrated in order to perceive the idea shining through it; the linguistic sense sweeps the mind along in irresistibly lively movement.
For it follows the fleetingness of thought and strives after its infinity.

Since every word belongs to a series, and none completely exhausts its concept, the linguistic sense passes from one to another and runs through the gradually unfolding sequence of thoughts, leaving behind it only the lightest breaks, those which least disturb by pauses the interrupted connection.

Where the obscure feeling of the constitution of the object is laid into the tone of the word, as firmness is in *Stärke* ['strength'], and in *Wolke* ['cloud'], *Wolle* ['wool'], *Wald* ['forest'] the wavering indeterminacy of the delimitation and of the coming together of the parts before the eye, there is indeed something symbolic in it.
For this constitution then shines forth from the tone, and the tone acts upon feeling like an image of it.
But the word-sound itself cannot on that account be called a symbol.
For its meaning, to which this symbolic part of it merely contributes, is not recognized from that, but by the quite different path which language in general takes.
Still more determinately and more frequently the symbolic lies in the concept of words, and precisely in that of which we are speaking here, their sensuous designation.
This is the case with all metaphorical expressions.
But this too does not alter the nature of the word.

This undeniable symbolizing on the part of language proves that a happy aptitude for it beneficially supports the linguistic sense; but it now also becomes completely clear in what relation the two stand to one another.

There must be the gift and the urge to seek out the sensuous and the non-sensuous in one another and to envelop them in one another, but the bright and clear orientation towards what is mental must predominate, and by the living strength of the power of thought must suppress the inclination to linger precisely at the obscure and mysterious connection of the two.

Since the sensuous presentation lying in the word and its self-meaning are here in question, the question arises what the soul actually presents to itself sensuously with the word: the object as a whole? or the properties apprehended in it in the word? or something indeterminate corresponding to the feeling aroused by the word? or, among peoples that have long possessed an alphabet, the written characters?
To explore this by self-observation would probably be difficult.
The intention already alters the object of observation, and certainly the presentation itself also varies, according to individuality and circumstances, through all those cases.

What, on the other hand, must be held fast not merely as certain but also as decisive for recognizing the true nature of language is that the word never brings the object into presentation otherwise, and never lets presentation dwell on it longer, than is required by the connection of thought of the moment, to which it subordinates the object and into which it weaves it as a link.

This lies in the nature of the word, which after all puts tones in the place of actual objects only in order to transform these, by this mediation, into thoughts; it lies further in the fact that the series of thoughts expressed by several words is, strictly taken,
one, and discourse a whole, in which the breaks always at the same time have the purpose of making the structure, as a whole, pre-eminently visible.
It is therefore one of the most important properties of the word to stimulate in presentation exactly that, and no more, which the use requires.
This is indeed brought about in large part by the appropriate connection with other determining words and by the whole orientation given to the soul of the hearer.

But it also lies in part in the formation of the word, which in this respect must possess purity, sharpness and sobriety in the determination of the concept, and full appropriateness to a clearly thought purpose.

From this there arises at the same time the necessity of several expressions for the same object according to the difference of use, in differing indication of the sides brought out in it, and in different moods of the soul.
For these too come into consideration here beside the logical purpose of discourse, and act pre-eminently on the kind of sensuous presentation lying in the word.
For the same word is evidently accompanied by different presentations in a poetic and in a scientific exposition.
Here too, however, language creates more by chance than by design, and the words of kindred sense are often only words carried over from other dialects with an accessory concept taken up into them.

The accompanying feeling (95.) acts on words either as a single sentiment of the heart, or as the collective mood of the combined intellectual powers and powers of the heart, where the former indeed rule but take on the colour of the latter.

From the former arise the caressing, honorific, solemn, scolding, contemptuous, mocking and jocular expressions; from the latter the poetic, the philosophical, the admonitory and moving, etc. Properly, no word is uttered without one of these nuances of sentiment, even though they are unnoticeable in the individual case, since the strings thereby set sounding always lie taut in the heart.

Here, however, we are speaking only of those particular words into whose formation these determinations of feeling have so passed that they now always arouse the same ones and, where these are out of place, cannot be used.
In the individual languages one perceives in these expressions a twofold remarkable phenomenon.
The languages of uncultivated peoples contain a great number of such expressions as betray a single sentiment of the heart.

Language always spiritualizes human beings, leads them first up to pure intellectuality, but then, if no counterweight comes in, beyond the summit to an intellectuality that is dry, sophistical and trifling; yet it does this only gradually.
All popular dialects make more frequent use of caressing, diminutive, augmentative and pejorative words than the higher, purified idiom.
On the other hand, one must not look there for specifically poetic ones; everything is still, in a certain measure, poetic, and is so received, without consciousness of the contrast.

In the languages of some highly cultivated nations, on the other hand, this consciousness is so fine and lively, and the diction so chaste, that a poetic word is never tolerated in unfettered discourse.

This springs only mediately from the nation's feeling for poetry, but immediately from its feeling for prose as a distinct genre of discourse, a feeling which presupposes a far more highly heightened and more finely refined linguistic sense.
It is therefore met with only in the noblest languages, and those most ingeniously cultivated.

Among philosophical words one must distinguish the merely logical ones, constructed by the understanding, which belong simply to the technical and scientific ones, from those that have arisen from deeper reflection or higher revelation, through synthesizing reason.
Where, as in the Indian language, abstract philosophy has entered into a grand union with the highest poetry, these expressions are found in pre-eminent strength and beauty.
In the foregoing I have tried to analyse the nature and the requirements of words, each considered singly by itself, in order to show how language designates the single concept.

It is now necessary to investigate the whole stock of the words of a single language in the relations of their meaning to one another, and with reference to the compass of objects and concepts, in order to show how language proceeds so as to create fitting expressions for every use in discourse, and to designate the whole mass of the concepts that occur.
Every language, whichever it may be, bears in its womb, at every point in time of its existence, the expression of all the concepts that can ever develop in the nation.
Each, further, is at any given point in time of its life exactly equal to the nation's compass of thought at that time.

Each, finally, in every one of its states forms the whole of a world-view, in that it contains expression for all the presentations which the nation forms for itself of the world, and for all the sentiments which the world produces in it.
These propositions rest on the identity of thinking and speaking.
Whatever human beings can think, that they are also able to say.

The thinking of a nation sometimes develops through mixture with another, in which case the language too receives foreign accretions; but it can also form itself entirely out of itself, and complete its whole course within itself, and nation and language, if this succeeds, thrive thereby the better and with a character more peculiarly their own.
The thinking of the nation, consisting of the thinking of each single person, must at every moment be a whole.

For it is the way in which human beings at every moment assert their mental existence in its stance towards the world; and since this whole existence, which consists only in this activity, necessarily contracts itself into every single act of thinking, this cannot happen piecemeal, nor in mutilated form.
Those propositions, however, are of the highest importance for the right appraisal of language.

For it rests on them that one regards language at no moment of its life as closed, but always as advancing, and everything contained in it as the germ of new development, and that one views its advance not mechanically, as an adding-on of parts, but truly organically, as an unfolding of a whole out of a whole.

The possibility of this nature of language lies in that of which mention has already been made in the foregoing: in the aptitude of articulated sounds for transpositions and combinations of every kind, where, through the production of small differences while a general resemblance persists, whole families of word-sonorities (79.) arise from a single basic sound; and through the deflection of the same word to kindred meanings, through the settling of the words that are in general of like meaning, and through the new stamping of words otherwise differently used.
It is a creating of tones and a creating of concepts through which language grows within itself; the latter goes on to infinity, but the former, as all experience shows, has a limit.
Language reaches a point where the wealth of sonorities is no longer increased from its own womb, but at most still through the adoption of foreign words.
The further elaboration then becomes, in a manner, more inward, and confines itself to the fixing and modifying of the meanings.
The lack of all historical experience forbids saying anything more precise about this dividing point.
This much, however, one can well see: that it lies where the coming together and mingling of the tribes with one another ceases, either in itself or in its influence upon language.

For every inner enlargement of language in its tones can, after all, properly be conceived only thus: that several who speak the same language bring differences into it, through peculiarity or separation, which then pass over into the whole, either already accompanied by differences of meaning as well, or receiving them only there.

Because everyone, in order to be understood, properly wants to speak as the other does, yet everyone, being after all physically and mentally another, in fact speaks somewhat differently, while this somewhat different speech is nevertheless understood and taken up again, a great variety of word-sonorities can arise in a language, if one imagines this going on for centuries among individuals, families and tribes.
That one dialect enriches another and the general language is, after all, something we often experience ourselves.
In so far as one understands by the wealth of a language its capacity to satisfy the need of expression, all may be called equally rich.
For as soon as one truly possesses a language, no concept and no turn of ideas can lack its appropriate designation.

The examination of the wealth of a language is not on that account an idle investigation, however, provided only that one is properly agreed about the sense of the expression; and there are indeed different degrees and kinds of this wealth.

What matters first is that every object or concept that sets itself apart definitely as a single one should also find in the language a single word that designates it without circumlocution; and likewise, secondly, that the objects should just as little lack the due diversity of expression according to the sentiment with which one speaks and the mode of intuition towards which one is working.
But, thirdly, there may also be several words for the same object without perceptible difference of meaning or intention, and fourthly, finally, several forms of the same word.

It is the case in all languages that what some express by a single word is rendered by others through a circumlocution of several, and the clarity and definiteness of the designation may nevertheless be the same.
It is nevertheless by no means a matter of indifference if a language must often take refuge in circumlocution.
The communication of thoughts, the momentary purpose of discourse, admittedly does not suffer thereby; but the difference lies in the form of the language, its reaction upon thinking in general.

For one must never forget that the constitution of language, as an instrument of thinking, exercises an immediate influence upon it, heightens or lowers its clarity, definiteness, rapidity and sharpness, gives it a sensuous direction outwards or a mental one inwards, and that this is by far the most important side of language.

Now where every concept finds the word destined for it, this wealth stimulates the mind; the language appears like the world, in which object likewise presses upon object, and like a world-view it is, after all, meant to place itself between nature and the human being.
I shall also return later to the point that it is of the highest importance that language, leaving the barren abstractness of thoughts, should take up into its form the form of external reality.
This is borne out here too.

Even a language poor in words can express a multitude of concepts and series of ideas, and can even do so with clarity and definiteness; one sees an example of this in the paltry use which some missionary writings make of non-European languages that are certainly richer in themselves.
Justice is then no doubt done to the content of the thought.
But the meagreness of the language drags the mind down, and thinking in such a representation lacks fullness, freshness and liveliness.

For the same reasons, several words for the same concept, even if they should present scarcely perceptible differences, and several forms of the same word, ought not to appear as a superfluous luxury.

They not only increase the sensuous fullness of the language, but also, in the advancing mental development of the nation, give occasion to shade the concepts more finely and to determine them more exactly, at least through the use of the different expressions, even if this cannot always be demonstrated in the dictionary.

Even when languages which, like English, have flowed together out of different ones possess for certain concepts two expressions differing merely in their origin, such as *freedom* and *liberty*, the use of these is nevertheless not wholly indifferent among orators of fine discernment and knowledge of the language.
In general, no kind of wealth in languages is to be held in low esteem.

Each proves that — whether this is to be ascribed to the duration of the language's existence, to the multitude of tribes and individuals who spoke it, or to the mental alertness of the nation — much was spoken in it and in manifold ways, and that consequently many thoughts and sentiments passed over into it.
But the more substance of human existence resounds towards the spirit of a language, the greater, livelier and more spiritual is its stimulating power.

In order to judge the constitution of a language completely with respect to its stock of words, one would have to compare this stock with the mass of possible concepts, what is designated with what is to be designated.

Understood of the pure concepts, this is impossible, since the material of thought cannot be purely separated from the material of language; rather, it is the designation that first completes the coming-into-being, before the mind, of what is to be designated.
This is the case even with natural objects, since the word, after all, designates not them as such, but the view of them that is grounded in the language.
This, however, concerns only strict and wholly exact analysis; otherwise one can certainly ask: which of them find, in a given language, expressions originally peculiar to it?
With non-sensuous concepts, however, this separation of word and concept is in part much less to be attempted, in part not to be attempted at all.
There is, however, an analogue by which the intended purpose can be attained at least to some extent.

One can, namely, put in the place of the concepts that are to be thought purely those actually designated in a number of languages, and measure the mass of what admits and demands designation by what, more or less, is usually designated in the various known languages.
To this extent the study of the existing languages serves for the examination of the compass of the thinking and sensibility that have actually existed in the human race.

If one now combines this method with the investigation of the pure material of thought, separated from any particular language, by means of the setting up of general categories of objects and concepts and of an ever-descending division, but with the constant consciousness that, where in this descent one arrives at the individual concept, a particular language must step in, then one can, without falling into errors, nevertheless hold the material of thought that is to be designated — not purely and completely, but sufficiently for the investigation of language — against the stock of words of a language.

Dictionaries arranged by categories, such as Pollux and Amara's Cosha, are useful aids to this end, and it was an apt idea of Havestadt's to arrange the words of the language of Chili in this way too.

But these works must be made much more complete, and one should not neglect to gather, from as many languages as it is possible to compare, the words by which objects are designated, or concepts stamped, that find in other languages no exhaustive expression in a word of their own.
I must indeed repeat here that, if one takes the matter sharply and exactly, no word of one language corresponds completely to that of another.
Here, however, we are speaking only of the cases where, through a word, a new concept, or a new and important nuance of a concept, really arises for those who did not previously know the language.

For what matters here is the discovery of the material of thought that is to be designated, and for this the mere advance by categories and logical definitions cannot suffice unless one adds to it what has already actually been thought in language.
