It can therefore be stated, and it must be stated, for which objects and concepts a language possesses words: what it has designated with words on earth and in the heavens, among lifeless and living things, on the animal and the human body, what, finally, among concepts of property and of relation, and what among non-sensuous concepts.

Where several languages have something in common, be it only through the like situation of the nations speaking them, as the American languages do, it becomes important to see whether roughly the same circle encloses the stock of the concepts stamped into words in them; and through the comparison of many languages one might well arrive — always starting from the principle that every language affords a whole of world-view — at a certain, as it were original, circle of this kind, recurring in all.

This circle would even have to be the same in all, since on the whole the same world exhibits itself to all nations, were it not that how much of this world is actually transformed into language depends on power and opportunity.

It is easily possible here to trace the progress of the discovery and naming of particular objects; but especially important is the search for the modifications of the mental concepts, a search which even in known languages has not yet been pursued nearly exactly enough.

Within the stock of words of a language there arises the further question: which genera of objects and concepts have a preponderance in the wealth of their expressions? and so in this respect too what matters is a sorting of them by classes.

For naturally it is not only the general state of cultivation of the nations that produces inequalities here; habit, custom and way of life also bestow a greater variety of expressions now on this, now on that branch of human occupation, and hence now on this, now on that class of objects and concepts.

The general investigation of language must not only start from the most general classes, but must also lay out its division in such a way that there results from it the manner in which language indicates the concept both before the understanding (98.) and before the ear — what may be called the technique of its designation.

Since for this one must follow language's own course, and all need of designation rests in thinking, all words divide, in this regard, into those that concern the matter, the object, and those that concern the form, the activity, of thinking.
For thinking needs words of its own in order to connect, to separate and to compare the concepts, and to treat them according to the operations peculiar to it.

These words may in general be called logical or dialectical, and their peculiarity consists in this: that, considered subjectively, they designate something produced by inner action, but, considered objectively, neither objects nor properties of objects, but only references and relations of concepts and things to one another, and to the understanding by which they are thought.
In the matter of thinking, the domain of the corporeal and the incorporeal naturally forms the principal division.
With regard to the technique of designation, however, it must be preceded by one that is more essential in this respect, namely that of the words for objects, qualities and actions.

For since objects always stimulate human beings through some salient peculiarity of quality or motion, they also prompt them to designate the objects chiefly by it, and words of quality and of motion therefore hover as the highest and most general in language.
The general words of relation and of reference must also be counted here.

For although, strictly, since it is the understanding that refers the concepts to one another, they fall into the class (117.) of the expressions designating its activity, yet in so far as one regards them as present in the objects themselves, they also belong here in this respect.
One might wish to object here that this distinction is a merely grammatical one.
But in all languages it is really lexical and grammatical at once.

For in all of them there are words which originally and by their concept — that is, lexically — are substantives, adjectives and adverbs, or verbs, even without any grammatical marks; and those which accordingly belong to one genus grammar afterwards transforms into the two other genera.

It is thus essential to note that in more than one language non-original verbs are formed merely by the combination of one original stem with another likewise original one — that is, purely lexically, and without any help from grammar.

To these main divisions all the particular ones now attach themselves, which, however, I pass over here, where I am endeavouring to give only the briefest possible sketch of the general structure of language.
This same classification of concepts now also facilitates and furthers insight into the technique of designation.

For I intend to speak of this here not with reference to the tones but (98.), remaining within the domain of thinking, of the choice of words for things and concepts according to other concepts singled out in them or referred to them.

These concepts can by no means always be recognized in the words; but to seek out those that are recognizable is uncommonly important, since not only does the individual world-view given through the language first shine forth quite distinctly from this, but also, in general, the whole mode of designation through kinship of concepts, subjective and objective, is one of the most wonderful sides of language.

For the task is nothing less than to ascend from the first and crudest needs of mutual communication to the totality of the highest ideas and their finest nuances, and always to attach the new word, or the new meaning, to something already present, since language always stands under the general condition of the possibility of mutual understanding, and the speaker therefore may not go beyond what has once been understood any further than the hearer is in a position to follow.

Language refers the incorporeal concepts to corporeal ones, and the beings of the corporeal world to the general categories of quality and motion; yet the latter rule is not as pervasive as the former.

From both it follows that there is present in language a number of general corporeal concepts of quality and of motion which form the chief material for the designation of all the rest, and for which one must therefore chiefly look when investigating the stock of words of a language.
One can therefore also conduct this investigation from two different sides: from the side of the designating concepts and from that of the concepts to be designated.

The comparison of this twofold procedure then shows in part the appropriateness of the designation, and in part, in the choice and determination of the designating concepts, the inclination prevailing in the people towards this or that sensuous mode of intuition, and the manner of its mental apprehension, the degree of its clarity, definiteness, purity and depth.
It is by no means necessary on that account that a language should possess a number of root-words which could be regarded as the origin of all the rest.
Even where such are present, derived words too are nevertheless used, and most frequently, for the designation of new concepts.
But the consideration of root-words cannot be bypassed here.
For they evidently have a twofold value, a grammatical and a lexical one.
They cannot appear in connected discourse at all, or only under certain conditions, without grammatical change, and they serve as stem-words for derivation and compounding.
There are languages, such as Sanskrit and Welsh, in which it has become lexicographical custom to trace every word back to one of the assumed roots.
But there is probably none of this structure in which the groundlessness of such a procedure could not be shown by striking examples.
Alongside the majority of words that can be derived willingly and easily from the roots, there are always still many that can be brought under them only by forced and playful artifice.
Language, however, also knows another means of increasing its wealth of words besides the formation of single expressions.

For it designates, on whole series of words, determinations common to them all; it creates expressions not through new word-sonorities but through alteration, determined according to rules, of those already present.
This often takes place through mere compounding, but also through derivation, and indeed both through agglutination and through inflection.

Of this kind are the patronymics, gentile nouns, abstract nouns, the ownership-words (a genus running through almost all the American languages), the causal and volitive verbs, and so forth. Since, for reasons very much to be approved in practice, one has by now become accustomed

to admit into the grammar everything that can be reduced to rules, and to leave to the dictionary only the alphabetical registering of the particular item, these methods of designation are now usually found in the grammars; but they evidently belong to the formation of the stock of words, not to the connection of discourse.
Their more exact and deeper investigation is important, however, because by it one can judge how logically exact and philosophically correct the language's procedure is in this.

For since we are speaking here of genera formed according to rules, what matters is how the principle of division has been apprehended, whether all the species flowing from it have been exhausted, and indeed even whether, in the choice of designating these concepts by derivation — that is, according to laws that must be learnt — or by compounding — that is, in an immediately intelligible way — chance or a rule has prevailed.

For it would be more in keeping with logical purposiveness to undertake formation according to laws only where the genera to be designated can, in number and constitution, be derived purely from concepts, not where, as with the concept of ownership, a single factual relation determines the genus of words.

There is yet another case in which the logical appropriateness and completeness of linguistic designation must be examined, namely in the concepts which together fill a sphere, where the question then is whether the language possesses an expression of its own for each of them, and whether the reciprocal reference of these concepts is designated in the expressions themselves.
As examples I need cite here only the dimensions of space and the cardinal points.

In the former, several languages comprise under the same expression two different ones, such as *schmal* ['narrow'] and *eng* ['tight, close'], *breit* ['broad'] and *gross* ['large']; in the latter, in many languages, as in German and Sanskrit (in German with reference to the course of the sun that divides the day, in Sanskrit with reference to an assumed standpoint from which the sides are determined), the expression preserves the uniformity of the concepts; in others, as in Latin, this uniformity is disturbed, or none at all is present.

The whole investigation of the stock of words of languages, here indicated only in barest outline, aims at recognizing the system of its formation as exactly and completely as possible, so that one may survey: how much, what among the given possibilities, and in what manner does the language designate?

Therefore the domain of what is to be designated must be gone through according to its various divisions (113–118.), then the stock of the concepts which are referred to others for the purpose of designation (119–122.), and finally the compass of the word-sounds, of the root-words as well as of the derived and compound ones, according to the constitution and treatment of the tones (73–82.).

Once this has been done, one possesses a concept of the materials which language offers to discourse, and has now only (105.) to consider the feeling that accompanies the words, their reaction upon the soul.
Hitherto this was spoken of only as a part of the word's substance; here, however, the peculiarity of the language in its treatment of all words is to be drawn together.
As the world appears in what is to be designated, so here the human being appears, and both referred to one another in the way in which both exhibit themselves in the same language.

The readier or more sluggish excitability of feeling, the brighter or darker colour of fancy, the more prosaic or more poetic direction become manifest here as causes, just as, in the objective formation of words, one recognized them as results.
It would therefore also be useless to enter further into particulars here.

It suffices to remark that what matters here is to consider subjectively the stock of words hitherto examined objectively, in order to see whether a certain uniformity of the feeling that prevailed in word-formation can be discovered, and what kind of national peculiarity reveals itself in it.
For this feeling, which acts upon the formation, is the same that afterwards always accompanies the word in use as well.

I call it feeling, however, partly in order to comprise in the most general word everything in which language can bear upon itself the traces of the human manner of being, but partly, and especially, because what we are speaking of here really operates, at the moment of its activity, only as feeling, not in clear and distinct consciousness.

For otherwise the purely intellectual direction too is very pre-eminently contained in it, as is the whole subjective effect which the words of one language, because they belong to it, produce differently from those of another.
That this in turn also contributes to the objective representation of the world through language goes without saying.
But many separations and divisions necessary in the science of language lead not so much to really different objects as merely to the consideration of different sides of the same object.

If, for example, there lies in the word-formation of a language the direction of keeping the mind by preference in the sphere of easy connection of ideas for the purposes of life, then it will be chiefly this intellectual mood that usually accompanies the incorporeal expressions of the language as well.
But at the same time it will result from this that these expressions themselves also, in the designation, take their objects more from the superficial side.

Nevertheless, in order to know the language completely from this side, the twofold setting side by side of this objective constitution and of this subjective influence upon it will always remain necessary.
For the latter will afterwards appear uniformly in other parts of the structure of language as well, notably, for example, in the joining together of discourse.

The subjective mood which co-operates in word-formation, and is produced again by the formed word, since cause and effect always step each into the other's place, clings far less firmly to the dead word than does the designation of the object.
If, then, even the latter, as we have seen (84.), is exposed to changes in the course of time, this is far more the case with the subjective impression.

Elevated words sink to common ones, poetic words become prosaic, and conversely; the whole direction of a nation's thinking and sensibility alters imperceptibly, and as this in turn (125.) reacts upon the designation, sound and meaning do indeed remain apparently and on the whole the same, but the altered apprehension of the latter nevertheless shows closer examination something different in it.

Thus, through mere apprehension, a very different sense is gradually slipped beneath incorporeal expressions in particular: *Seele* ['soul'], *Geist* ['mind, spirit'], *Herz* ['heart'], *Gemüth* ['mind, temper'], and so forth.

Conversely, however, as this happens in some principal expressions, perhaps through the influence of individual writers, the mental direction of the nation gradually alters, and this change then reacts in intensified proportion upon the whole language.
Of these changes in the feeling that accompanies the words, whether or not they exert influence on their meanings, the isolated words seldom bear any recognizable traces.
Only where literary monuments exist can they be traced.

Since, moreover, the causes of these changes lie solely in the nation's mode of apprehension, while very sudden and abrupt transitions are possible within the human being, languages undergo these transformations — the most decisive precisely for their innermost essence — more quickly, more frequently and more strongly than those brought about through deflection even of the meanings as a whole, and through reshaping of the tones.

Their study belongs chiefly to the history of the cultivation of the mind; the study of language often leaves them lying wholly outside its circle, and does no wrong in this if it wishes to confine itself merely to the material, as it were cruder, part of language, but must necessarily include it within itself if language, as is the aim here, is to be represented in its complete relation to the human being.

notes.issue: Pronouns *durch sie* / *in ihr* follow the plural *der Sprachen* but *ihr* is singular; I refer both to 'a language'. *Vorstellungsart* = 'mode of presentation', *Vorstellungsweise* (p75:s4) = 'manner of presentation', *Auffassung* = 'apprehension'. In p75:s4 the word means little more than 'view'.
alternatives: the mode of presentation given through them than from the sounds used in it
p75:s4: 'The view that regards these languages ... is entirely false'

notes.issue: This is the 1906 editor's footnote, not the author's. No label is added in the English because the ID carries the authorship. The journal title is left untranslated and without asterisks, which are reserved for mentioned forms.
*Betonungsarten* refers to the Chinese tones (called *Intonationen* in §66). I avoid 'tones' because *Ton* is 'tone' in the main text.
alternatives: all the existing modes of accentuation

notes.issue: *Gattung* is rendered 'genus' (also p79:s2), following the natural-history analogy of §§7–8 and keeping it distinct from *Classification* (p75:s2).

The checked German has *im Verstände* (also in §§116–117). I read it as *im Verstande*, 'in the understanding', taking the umlaut as a transcription or OCR artefact. Worth checking against the page image.
*stellt sich ... her* is taken as 'rights itself / is restored', as the result clause requires (the same phenomenon as where no disproportion exists). The reading 'establishes itself' seems excluded.
alternatives: a disproportion is usually made good again by other circumstances

notes.issue: Possible textual problem. Literally the circumstances are harder to judge 'as they presuppose no exact knowledge' of living delivery (*keine genaue Kenntniss ... voraussetzen*). The sense expected is that judging them requires such knowledge, or that such knowledge cannot be assumed. I translate the checked text literally and do not emend; please verify *keine* against the image or manuscript.
alternatives: as they presuppose an exact knowledge of the living delivery (if *eine* is the true reading)
as no exact knowledge of the living delivery can be presupposed for them

notes.issue: *über ihren historischen oder physiologischen Unterschied*: the antecedent of *ihren* is unclear (the identity or kinship, the word-sounds, or the languages). I keep the literal 'difference' and refer it to the identity or kinship, i.e. whether the resemblance is historical or merely physiological (cf. §47). *Verwandtschaft* = 'kinship', *verwandt* = 'kindred' throughout.
alternatives: cannot by itself decide whether it is historical or physiological
decide as to their historical or physiological difference (of the word-sounds)

notes.issue: *Anklang* is rendered 'assonance', which is not the technical prosodic sense. *Anhängung, Vorschlag, Einschiebung* = 'suffixing, prefixing, insertion'. *der einfachere* is masculine, so I supply 'tone'.
alternatives: by appending, prefixing or inserting a sound

notes.issue: *durch die Vocalreihe*: literally 'through the series of vowels', apparently vowel alternation along the vowel scale; not modernized to 'ablaut'. *Sylbenwiederholungen und Versetzungen*: it is unclear whether the transpositions are of syllables only, so the ambiguity is kept.
alternatives: the repetitions and transpositions of syllables

notes.issue: *mehrerer von diesen*: the antecedent is loose; presumably several languages of the kind just described (those taken from an already formed language).
alternatives: in the vocabulary of several such languages

notes.issue: *womit sie in Berührung steht*: *sie* may be the generation of language or the nation; the English 'it' keeps the ambiguity. *Empfindung* (p79:s4) is rendered 'sensation' to keep it apart from *Gefühl* = 'feeling'.

*Gleichartigkeit* / *gleichartig* is rendered 'likeness in kind' / 'alike in kind' / 'of like kind' (p80:s3–s6, p81:s1, p81:s5, Coptic note), kept distinct from *Aehnlichkeit* 'similarity', *Einerleiheit* 'identity', *Gleichheit* 'sameness' and *Gleichförmigkeit* 'uniformity'.
*ohne Fortbildung durch sie*: *sie* is taken as the other nation; grammatically it could also be the analogies.
alternatives: and therefore without further development by means of them

notes.issue: Cited forms are kept exactly as transcribed (*hrosch*, *horsch*, *rôsha*, *hloili*, *loili*, *hroyr*, *hoyrooy*, *heri*), including the German-style *sch*. The syntax of *wie hroyr aus hoyrooy und heri entstanden* is compressed; I take *hroyr* as derived from both following forms. *Indisch* is kept as 'Indian'.

The bracketed glosses ['to lay'], ['to lie'] are translator's additions, not in the source; delete them if additions are unwanted. Greek forms are given asterisks under the general rule for mentioned forms, though Greek is usually not italicized.
*unter ihnen*: literally 'among them'; presumably between sounds and concepts.
*Phantasie* is rendered 'fantasy' to keep it distinct from *Einbildungskraft* = 'imagination' (p83:s1). *Scharfsinn* = 'ingenuity'.
*Wesen* is rendered 'entity' to avoid a clash with 'human being'.

*im Deutschen, und den von ihm abhängenden Sprachen*: rendered literally. The author may mean German in a wide, Germanic sense, with 'dependent' meaning derived or descended languages; the claim is left as his.
alternatives: in German and the languages deriving from it
in Germanic and the languages descended from it

notes.issue: Humboldt's three sound-terms are kept apart throughout: *Laut* 'sound', *Ton* 'tone', *Schall* 'audible sound' (p91:s12, p98:s9); *Wortlaut* is 'word-sound'. 'Tone' is not meant musically or as lexical tone. *Abbeugung* is 'deflection', *Stamm* 'tribe'.
*Gehalt* is rendered 'import' and kept distinct from *Inhalt* 'content' (p97:s1, p98:s3, p98:s9). *Stoff* is 'material' and *Materie* 'matter', because §90 makes *Materie*/*Form* a technical pair.

The source uses both *Gegenstand* and the Latinate *Object* (p85:s4 'der Gegenstand aber, als Object'). I render *Gegenstand* 'object' and *Object* capitalized 'Object' so that the pair stays visible. Related choices: *Vorstellung* 'presentation' (*sich vorstellen* 'present to itself'), *Vorstellungsweise* 'mode of presentation', *Auffassung* 'apprehension', *Anschauungsweise* 'mode of intuition', *Ansicht* 'view', *darstellen* 'portray', *stätig* (= stetig) 'continuous'.
alternatives: Object: lower-case 'object' with the German in brackets

notes.issue: *Geist*/*geistig* are rendered 'mind'/'mental' to keep them apart from *intellectuell* 'intellectual' and *Seele* 'soul'. English lacks matching derivatives, so *vergeistigen* is 'spiritualize' (p89:s1, p105:s6) and *Geistigkeit* 'spirituality' (p89:s3); *das Geistige* is 'what is mental'. *geistreich* and *geistvoll* are both 'ingenious(ly)'. *körperlich* is 'corporeal'.

*Empfindung* is rendered 'sentiment' to distinguish it from *Gefühl* 'feeling', hence 'thinking and sentiment' for *Denken und Empfinden* (p93:s3) and 'validity for sentiment' for *Empfindungsgeltung* (p89:s4). *Gemüth* (p105) is 'heart', so *Gemüthskräfte* is 'powers of the heart'. *bestimmt*/*Bestimmung*/*Bestimmtheit* are 'determinate'/'determination'/'determinacy', except *Bestimmung* 'vocation' at p101:s12.
Each *es* in the series of *dass*-clauses is taken as *das Wort*, not *der Gegenstand*; I supply 'the word itself' once for clarity.
alternatives: keep 'it' throughout and leave the reference open

notes.issue: *Weite* is rendered 'breadth' here, at p91:s12 (*Spielraum bequemer Weite*) and at p92:s3 (*zwiefache Weite der Lautform*). The neuter *jedes* has no explicit antecedent; I leave it as 'each … its own', understanding each individual or individuality having its own language.
alternatives: 'each individual can nevertheless have a language of its own'

notes.issue: *die Wirkung desselben* could refer to the word, the tone or the concept. 'Its effect' keeps this open; I incline to the word.

*sinnliche Geltung* is rendered 'sensuous validity'. *Geltung*/*galt* are 'validity'/'had validity' throughout (p88:s1, p89:s4, p101:s15). *sinnlich* is 'sensuous' and *unsinnlich* 'non-sensuous', except 'sense perception' and 'objects of sense'.

The masculine *ihn … er* in the parenthesis refers to *des Bezeichneten*, i.e. the bearer of the proper name; I use neutral 'what is designated … it'. *zusammenfassen* is 'gather together' wherever the word's gathering of an object is meant (p95:s1, p98:s6, p89:s6). The checked text reads *dem Räume* here and *2u* at p88:s3; I read *Raume* and *zu*.
*indem es die Individualitaet der Sprechenden war* is terse. I take *es* as resuming *Beides* (matter and form, as what was once the speakers' individuality).
alternatives: 'in being the individuality of the speakers, it attached itself to the sounds'
'since it was the individuality of the speakers'

notes.issue: The German says *zu Adjectiven gewordene Substantiva* ('substantives that have become adjectives'). The argument, and p93:s4 (*Substantiva zu sichtlich aus Adjectiven bildend*), suggest the reverse was intended. I translate what is printed; this needs checking against the manuscript.
alternatives: 'adjectives that have become substantives' (only if the editor emends)

notes.issue: The cited form *dwîpa* and the etymologies are kept as the author gives them. The bracketed single-quoted glosses after German example words here and at p98:s10 and p103:s1 are my additions and can be stripped. *Indisch* is 'Indian' ('the Indian language' at p105:s13), not 'Sanskrit'.
alternatives: move the glosses to translator's notes

notes.issue: The cross-reference '(90.)' is kept as printed, although the designation of objects by their properties is discussed in §91. In *in dieser auch mit Selbständigkeit begabte Wörter* I take *in dieser* as 'in nature', going with *selbständiger Wesen*.
alternatives: take *in dieser* as 'in language': 'must use in it words likewise endowed with self-subsistence'

notes.issue: *Nicht leicht werden zwei Sprachen … halten* may mean either that hardly any two languages strike the same balance, or that languages rarely keep a perfect balance among the stimuli. The literal rendering leaves this open.
alternatives: 'Hardly any two languages will keep, in the form of their words, the same perfect equilibrium …'

notes.issue: *Vieldeutigkeit* is 'multiplicity of meanings' (p97:s4, p97:s6), distinguished from *Vielfachheit* 'plurality' (p97:s8) and *vielumfassender Umfang* 'comprehensive extent'. *Nebenbegriff*/*Nebenbedeutung* are 'accessory concept'/'accessory meaning'.
*Selbstbedeutung* is the author's own coinage (*könnte man … nennen*), so I calque it as 'self-meaning' (p99, p104:s1).
*nicht an sich* is elliptical. I read it as 'not [separable from sound] in itself, i.e. absolutely', contrasted with separation from the particular sound proper to it in one language.

Authorship: note:deleted-word-symbol and note:deleted-images-signs are the 1906 editor's notes reporting passages Humboldt deleted in the manuscript; the quoted matter is Humboldt's. The cue words *sich* and *zusammen* are left in German because they are the final words of p101:s7 and p101:s8 in the source. The other four notes in this block are Humboldt's own.

*tropisch* is rendered 'tropical' in the rhetorical sense (pertaining to tropes), and *Darstellungsart* 'mode of portrayal'. The title is left in German as cited. The run-on punctuation between the two quotations follows the source.
'(h. v.)' is kept as printed; it is presumably *hac voce*, the equivalent of 's.v.'. The Greek is left untranslated.

The checked text reads *Weile*, which I render 'measure of lingering'. The deleted note's *verweilend* supports it, but a misreading of *Weise* ('manner') cannot be excluded without the manuscript. *Bildung der Köpfe* is 'formation of intellects'.
alternatives: 'a quite different pace in the succession of presentations'
if *Weise*: 'a quite different manner in the succession of presentations'

notes.issue: *Einschnitte* is 'breaks' here and at p104:s6. The antecedent of *er* is *der Sprachsinn*, which I make explicit.
The checked text reads *Gäbe*; I translate *Gabe* ('gift'), taking the umlaut as an OCR artefact.

The segmentation splits one sentence between p104:s5 and p104:s6 (*genau genommen.* / *Eins, und die Rede …*); the full stop is evidently a misread comma. The English follows the IDs, so p104:s5 ends on a comma and p104:s6 begins in lower case.
alternatives: merge the two IDs: '… is, strictly taken, one, and discourse a whole, in which …'

notes.issue: *von verschiedenen* is elliptical; I supply 'presentations' from the preceding sentence. *Vortrag* is 'exposition' here and 'diction' at p105:s9. *Rede* is 'discourse' throughout.
This ID contains two sentences (*… u. s. f. Es wird eigentlich …*); both are translated under it. *ermahnend rührenden* is taken as one compound type of expression.
*fesselfreie Rede* is rendered literally as 'unfettered discourse'. It means prose (cf. *oratio soluta*), which the next sentence names explicitly.

Terminology held constant across the block: Vorrath der Wörter / Wortvorrath / Wörtervorrath = 'stock of words' (so that it stays parallel with 'Vorrath der Begriffe', 'stock of concepts', in §§115 and 123); Rede = 'discourse'; Umfang = 'compass'; bezeichnen / Bezeichnung = 'designate / designation'. Cross-references such as '(79.)' are left in the source's form.
alternatives: 'vocabulary' for Wörtervorrath, as in the division heading

notes.issue: Vorstellung = 'presentation', and Darstellung is kept apart as 'representation' (§§111, 125, 126) or 'exhibit itself' for sich darstellen (§§115, 124). Empfindung = 'sentiment' and Empfinden = 'sensibility' (§§113, 126), so that 'feeling' is reserved for Gefühl, which Humboldt defines as a term in §125.
alternatives: 'thinking and feeling' for Denken und Empfinden

notes.issue: Generic 'der Mensch' is rendered 'human beings' (plural) here and in p108:s5 and p118:s3 to avoid a gendered singular pronoun; elsewhere 'the human being'. Geist is 'mind' and geistig 'mental' throughout, except p112:s6.
alternatives: 'spirit / spiritual' or 'intellect / intellectual' (the latter collides with Humboldt's own 'intellectuell')

notes.issue: Three points. (1) Klang is kept distinct from Laut ('sound') and Ton ('tone') as 'sonority', hence Wortklänge = 'word-sonorities' against Wortlaute = 'word-sounds' (§123). (2) The syntax is loose: 'und durch die Abbeugung ...' has no governing verb parallel to 'liegt in'; I have kept the looseness. (3) 'Festsetzung der allgemein gleichbedeutenden Wörter' is unclear: it may mean settling (differentiating) words that are broadly synonymous, or establishing words as generally equivalent.
alternatives: 'the establishing of the generally synonymous words'

notes.issue: 'desselben' could grammatically refer to 'Ausdruck' or to 'Reichthum'. The four kinds listed next are kinds of wealth, so I have written 'of this wealth'.
'Redner' is rendered 'orators' because Humboldt elsewhere uses 'der Redende' for the ordinary speaker; the neutral sense is also possible.

Gattung is rendered 'kind' here, since it resumes the 'Grade und Arten' of wealth in p110:s3, but 'genus' in the classificatory passages (§§116, 118, 122), where it contrasts with Art = 'species' and Classe = 'class'.
alternatives: 'no genus of the wealth of languages'

notes.issue: Real doubt. As printed, 'dem Geiste einer Sprache' is a genitive ('towards the spirit of a language'), and I have translated that. But the parallel in p100:s2 ('dem beobachtenden Geiste ... entgegenstrahlt') and the following 'ihre anregende Kraft' suggest the sense 'resounds to the mind out of a language', which would need a preposition (aus / in) that the checked text does not have. This should be checked against the manuscript. It is also the one place where Geist / geistig is 'spirit / spiritual' rather than 'mind / mental'. Gehalt = 'substance', Inhalt = 'content'.
alternatives: 'But the more the substance of human existence resounds to the mind from a language, the greater, livelier and more mental is its stimulating power.'

notes.issue: The historical forms 'Pollux', 'Amara's Cosha' and 'Chili' are kept as cited. 'Auch auf diese Weise' is taken as 'in this way too', i.e. in addition to another arrangement, not 'Havestadt too'.
alternatives: 'it was also an apt idea of Havestadt's to arrange ...'

notes.issue: This footnote is by the 1906 editor, not Humboldt; I have marked that with a bracketed label, which is my addition. 'Oben S. 18 Anm.' refers to the pagination of the 1906 volume and will need adjusting or annotating in the edition.
alternatives: Drop the bracketed label if authorship is carried by metadata

notes.issue: 'Geistige Begriffe' is rendered 'mental concepts' (concepts of things of the mind, as against names of particular objects).

'Ihrer Ausdrücke' may be 'their' (the genera's) or 'its' (the language's) expressions, and 'derselben' may refer to the objects and concepts or to the expressions. The source's question mark is kept by casting the question as direct, as also in p113:s4 and p123:s1; in p125:s2 the question mark after an indirect question is normalized to a full stop.

'Allgemein logische oder dialektische' is ambiguous between 'call them, in general, logical or dialectical' and 'general-logical'. Beziehung = 'reference' and Verhältniss = 'relation' throughout (so 'Verhältniss- und Beziehungswörter' = 'words of relation and of reference').
alternatives: 'These words may be called general-logical or dialectical'

notes.issue: Beschaffenheit is 'quality' where it names the category paired with motion or action (§§118, 120), but 'constitution' where it means the make-up of a language or of the tones (§§111, 113, 122, 123, 125). Eigenschaft is 'property'.

Two doubts. (1) 'Es ist so wesentlich hierauf zu achten, dass ...': I take 'so' as 'thus' and the dass-clause as what is to be noted; a consecutive 'so ... that' gives no clear sense. (2) 'Eines ursprünglichen mit einem gleichfalls ursprünglichen Stamm': I take 'Stamm' as understood with both adjectives; grammatically the first could instead be '[Verbum]'.
alternatives: 'It is all the more essential to attend to this, in that in more than one language ...'
'by the combination of an original verb with a likewise original stem'

notes.issue: Geltung is rendered 'value'.
'Wallisisch' is taken as the older German name for Welsh, where root-based lexicography was current. It is not the dialect of the Valais.

The segmentation breaks a sentence: 'Da man sich ... einmal gewöhnt hat.' continues directly into p122:s5 ('Alles, was sich auf Regeln bringen lässt ...'), and the full stop after 'hat' looks like a transcription or segmentation artefact for a comma. My English for s4 therefore ends without a full stop and s5 begins in lower case; the two should be read together. Also: Eigenthumswörter = 'ownership-words' ('property' being reserved for Eigenschaft); Gentilitia = 'gentile nouns'.
'Weltgegenden' is rendered 'cardinal points'.

The German dimension-words are kept as cited forms with bracketed glosses of my own, because English cannot reproduce the schmal / eng pairing with single unambiguous words; the checked text shows no emphasis, though the uncorrected OCR suggests spaced type. 'In jenem ... in diesem' inside the parenthesis is resolved as German and Sanskrit respectively. 'Zwei verschiedne' is left as 'two different ones' (dimensions or concepts).
alternatives: 'narrow and tight, broad and large' without the German

notes.issue: 'Sie bezeichnet' is singular although 'der Sprachen' precedes; I render 'the language'.
Phantasie is rendered 'fancy' to keep it apart from Einbildungskraft ('imagination') earlier in the division. 'Erfolge' is 'results' in the older sense, not 'successes'.
Stimmung is rendered 'mood' here and in p126:s1.
The four German words are kept as cited forms, since the point is the shifting sense of these very words; the bracketed glosses are mine and only approximate, especially for Gemüth.
alternatives: Gloss Gemüth as 'heart and mind' or 'temperament'

notes.issue: 'Als die durch Abbeugung auch der Bedeutungen im Ganzen' is compressed: 'auch' may mean 'even' or 'likewise', and 'im Ganzen' may mean 'on the whole' or 'as wholes'. 'Abbeugung' is 'deflection' as in p109:s3.
alternatives: 'than those through the deflection of the meanings too, on the whole, and through the reshaping of the tones'

notes.issue: 'Muss ihn aber nothwendig in sich fassen': the masculine 'ihn' has no fitting antecedent (grammatically only 'Theil' or 'Kreis'), whereas the sense requires the study of these transformations ('es') or the transformations themselves ('sie'). I have translated with a neutral 'it' and not emended. This should be checked against the manuscript. Sprachkunde = 'the study of language', Sprachwissenschaft = 'science of language' (§125); Geistesbildung = 'cultivation of the mind'.
